{"parentUuid":"62692a4d-33ba-416f-a025-52ee09041c20","isSidechain":false,"promptId":"75407f73-9e26-4820-abc4-09e2bd0e1856","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_016jZN73EiuMCcMk6Di37Rup","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Technical Decisions — Phase 06: Inscrição em Canais (Subscriptions)\n2\t\n3\t> **Phase:** 06 — Interações Sociais (recorte: Inscrição em Canais)\n4\t> **Status:** Finalized\n5\t> **Date:** 2026-06-23\n6\t\n7\t---\n8\t\n9\t> **Scope note.** Phase 06 in `project-plan.md` covers likes, comments, and\n10\t> subscriptions. This document only addresses **channel subscriptions\n11\t> (follow/unfollow)** — the only Phase 06 capability that does not depend on the\n12\t> video entity (Phases 03–05, not implemented). Likes and comments operate on\n13\t> videos and are out of scope. Decisions here build only on Phase 02 (`User`,\n14\t> `Channel`, global `JwtAuthGuard`, domain exception filter).\n15\t\n16\t## TD-01: Subscription Persistence Model\n17\t\n18\t**Context:** A subscription links one authenticated user to one channel they\n19\tfollow. We need a persistence shape that enforces \"one subscription per\n20\t(user, channel)\" and supports both the \"channels I follow\" listing and the\n21\t\"subscriber count\" of a channel. Affects the data model and every endpoint.\n22\t\n23\t**Options:**\n24\t\n25\t### Option A: Dedicated `Subscription` join entity (user_id, channel_id, created_at)\n26\t- A new `subscriptions` table with its own UUID PK, FKs to `users` and\n27\t  `channels`, a `created_at`, and a unique constraint on `(user_id, channel_id)`.\n28\t  Each follow is one row; unfollow deletes the row.\n29\t- **Pros:** Mirrors the Phase 02 entity-per-concern style. Unique constraint\n30\t  enforces idempotency at the DB level. `created_at` enables \"recently followed\"\n31\t  ordering. Subscriber count is a simple `COUNT(*) WHERE channel_id = ?`.\n32\t  Natural place for future per-subscription metadata (notifications, muted).\n33\t- **Cons:** One extra table and module. Slightly more code than a counter column.\n34\t\n35\t### Option B: `@ManyToMany` join table managed by TypeORM\n36\t- Model the relation as `User.subscribedChannels` `@ManyToMany(() => Channel)`\n37\t  with a `@JoinTable`. TypeORM owns the implicit junction table.\n38\t- **Pros:** Less explicit entity code. TypeORM generates the join table.\n39\t- **Cons:** The implicit junction table has no `created_at` and no addressable\n40\t  entity, so \"recently followed\" ordering and future metadata are impossible\n41\t  without migrating to an explicit entity later. Harder to write a clean\n42\t  `COUNT` and to attach domain rules (self-subscription) at the service layer.\n43\t  Diverges from the project's explicit-entity convention.\n44\t\n45\t### Option C: Denormalized `subscriber_count` column on `channels`\n46\t- Add a counter column to `channels`, incremented/decremented on follow/unfollow,\n47\t  plus a separate table only to know *who* follows whom.\n48\t- **Pros:** O(1) subscriber count read.\n49\t- **Cons:** Two sources of truth that can drift under concurrency; needs\n50\t  transactional increment and is overkill for the current scale. Still needs a\n51\t  join table for the listing. Premature optimization.\n52\t\n53\t**Recommendation:** **Option A** — an explicit `Subscription` entity matches the\n54\tproject's conventions (one entity per concern, explicit columns, UUID PK,\n55\ttimestamps), enforces uniqueness in the DB, and keeps both reads\n56\t(listing + count) trivial. The count can be denormalized later if profiling\n57\tjustifies it.\n58\t\n59\t**Decision:** A (dedicated `Subscription` join entity)\n60\t\n61\t---\n62\t\n63\t## TD-02: Duplicate Subscribe Behavior (idempotent vs. conflict)\n64\t\n65\t**Context:** `POST /channels/:channelId/subscription` may be called when the user\n66\talready follows the channel. The unique constraint from TD-01 guarantees no\n67\tduplicate row, but the API must decide what HTTP outcome the caller sees.\n68\t\n69\t**Options:**\n70\t\n71\t### Option A: Conflict — 409 `ALREADY_SUBSCRIBED`\n72\t- The service checks for an existing subscription (or catches the unique\n73\t  violation) and throws a domain exception mapped to 409.\n74\t- **Pros:** Explicit, testable signal that the state already existed. Consistent\n75\t  with Phase 02's domain-error style (`EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS` is the same shape:\n76\t  a uniqueness conflict surfaced as 409). The frontend can distinguish \"you just\n77\t  followed\" from \"you already followed\" if it ever needs to.\n78\t- **Cons:** The client must tolerate a 409 on a double-click; strictly, a\n79\t  follow button is naturally idempotent from the user's mental model.\n80\t\n81\t### Option B: Idempotent — 201/204 always, no error on repeat\n82\t- Repeat calls silently succeed, returning the same success as the first.\n83\t- **Pros:** Friendliest for a toggle button; double-clicks never error.\n84\t- **Cons:** Hides state from the API contract; \"created\" vs \"already existed\"\n85\t  becomes indistinguishable. Inconsistent with how Phase 02 models uniqueness\n86\t  conflicts (it raises 409 rather than swallowing).\n87\t\n88\t**Recommendation:** **Option A** — surface the conflict as **409\n89\t`ALREADY_SUBSCRIBED`**, mirroring `EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS`. POST creates a\n90\tresource; a second creation of the same resource is a conflict. This keeps the\n91\tcontract explicit and aligns with the existing error-catalog philosophy.\n92\t(Note the deliberate asymmetry with TD-03: POST-create is *not* idempotent,\n93\tDELETE *is* — each follows its own REST semantics.)\n94\t\n95\t**Decision:** A (409 `ALREADY_SUBSCRIBED`)\n96\t\n97\t---\n98\t\n99\t## TD-03: Unsubscribe of a Non-existent Subscription (idempotent vs. error)\n100\t\n101\t**Context:** `DELETE /channels/:channelId/subscription` may be called when the\n102\tuser is not subscribed (never followed, or already unfollowed).\n103\t\n104\t**Options:**\n105\t\n106\t### Option A: Idempotent — 204 No Content regardless\n107\t- If no subscription exists, the endpoint still returns 204; the post-condition\n108\t  (\"the user does not follow this channel\") already holds.\n109\t- **Pros:** Matches REST semantics for DELETE — deleting an absent resource\n110\t  leaves the system in the requested state, so it is not an error. Robust to\n111\t  double-clicks and retries. Simplest client contract for a toggle.\n112\t- **Cons:** The caller cannot tell \"I just unfollowed\" from \"there was nothing\n113\t  to unfollow\" (acceptable for a follow toggle).\n114\t\n115\t### Option B: Error — 404 `SUBSCRIPTION_NOT_FOUND`\n116\t- Throw when there is no row to delete.\n117\t- **Pros:** Explicit signal that nothing was deleted.\n118\t- **Cons:** Punishes the common retry/double-click case with an error;\n119\t  contradicts DELETE idempotency. The channel-not-found case (TD-04) already\n120\t  covers the genuinely-wrong-target scenario.\n121\t\n122\t**Recommendation:** **Option A** — **204 idempotent**. DELETE is idempotent by\n123\tREST convention: the desired end state (\"not following\") is reached whether or\n124\tnot a row existed. This pairs intentionally with TD-02 (POST-create conflicts,\n125\tDELETE does not).\n126\t\n127\t**Decision:** A (204 idempotent — no error when not subscribed)\n128\t\n129\t---\n130\t\n131\t## TD-04: Self-subscription Prevention\n132\t\n133\t**Context:** The scope forbids a user from subscribing to their own channel. We\n134\tneed to decide where the check lives and which error it produces. Each user owns\n135\texactly one channel (Phase 02, `channels.user_id` unique).\n136\t\n137\t**Options:**\n138\t\n139\t### Option A: Service-layer check comparing channel owner to current user — 409 `CANNOT_SUBSCRIBE_TO_OWN_CHANNEL`\n140\t- The subscribe flow loads the target channel, compares `channel.user_id` to the\n141\t  authenticated `userId`, and throws a domain exception if they match.\n142\t- **Pros:** Business rule lives in the service (per `nestjs-layer-separation`).\n143\t  Reuses the channel lookup already needed for the 404 check (TD-05), so no\n144\t  extra query. Domain error is explicit and testable. 409 expresses \"the request\n145\t  conflicts with an invariant of the target resource\".\n146\t- **Cons:** Requires the channel's owner to be known at subscribe time (already\n147\t  loaded for the existence check, so effectively free).\n148\t\n149\t### Option B: Guard/DB-level prevention\n150\t- Encode the rule in a guard or a DB `CHECK` constraint.\n151\t- **Pros:** Centralized at the boundary.\n152\t- **Cons:** A guard embedding this comparison would leak business logic into the\n153\t  infrastructure layer (forbidden by `nestjs-layer-separation`). A DB `CHECK`\n154\t  cannot compare across tables (owner lives on `channels`, not on the\n155\t  subscription row) without a trigger — overkill.\n156\t\n157\t**Recommendation:** **Option A** — check in the service and throw **409\n158\t`CANNOT_SUBSCRIBE_TO_OWN_CHANNEL`**, reusing the channel lookup from the\n159\texistence check. All endpoints are protected by the global\n200\t`JwtAuthGuard`.\n201\t\n202\t**Options:**\n203\t\n204\t### Option A: Rely on login-time confirmation gate — no extra check\n205\t- Phase 02 `login` throws `EmailNotConfirmedException` (403) when\n206\t  `is_confirmed = false`, so an unconfirmed user can never obtain an access\n207\t  token. By the time a request carries a valid JWT, the account was confirmed at\n208\t  login. Therefore subscription endpoints need no additional confirmation check.\n209\t- **Pros:** No redundant logic; single source of truth for the confirmation gate\n210\t  (login). No duplicated `is_confirmed` checks spread across feature modules.\n211\t  Matches how every other authenticated endpoint in the project behaves.\n212\t- **Cons:** If a future change issued tokens before confirmation, this assumption\n213\t  would need revisiting (documented here so it is explicit).\n214\t\n215\t### Option B: Re-check `is_confirmed` in the subscription service — 403\n216\t- Load the user and reject unconfirmed accounts again at subscribe time.\n217\t- **Pros:** Defense in depth if token issuance ever changes.\n218\t- **Cons:** Redundant today (unconfirmed users cannot log in), adds a query and\n219\t  a branch with no observable effect, and spreads the confirmation rule outside\n220\t  auth.\n221\t\n222\t**Recommendation:** **Option A** — **no extra check**. Confirmation is enforced\n223\tonce, at login; a valid access token already implies a confirmed account. This\n224\tis documented as an explicit assumption rather than re-implemented per feature.\n225\t\n226\t**Decision:** A (no extra confirmation check — enforced at login)\n227\t\n228\t---\n229\t\n230\t## TD-07: How the Subscriber Count Is Exposed\n231\t\n232\t**Context:** The scope requires a channel's subscriber count to be reachable\n233\t(\"contagem de inscritos na página do canal\"), and leaves the exact shape to this\n234\tdecision. This document only addresses **channel subscriptions\n> (follow/unfollow)** — the only Phase 06 capability that does not depend on the\n> video entity (Phases 03–05, not implemented). Likes and comments operate on\n> videos and are out of scope. Decisions here build only on Phase 02 (`User`,\n> `Channel`, global `JwtAuthGuard`, domain exception filter).\n\n## TD-01: Subscription Persistence Model\n\n**Context:** A subscription links one authenticated user to one channel they\nfollow. We need a persistence shape that enforces \"one subscription per\n(user, channel)\" and supports both the \"channels I follow\" listing and the\n\"subscriber count\" of a channel. Affects the data model and every endpoint.\n\n**Options:**\n\n### Option A: Dedicated `Subscription` join entity (user_id, channel_id, created_at)\n- A new `subscriptions` table with its own UUID PK, FKs to `users` and\n  `channels`, a `created_at`, and a unique constraint on `(user_id, channel_id)`.\n  Each follow is one row; unfollow deletes the row.\n- **Pros:** Mirrors the Phase 02 entity-per-concern style. Unique constraint\n  enforces idempotency at the DB level. `created_at` enables \"recently followed\"\n  ordering. Subscriber count is a simple `COUNT(*) WHERE channel_id = ?`.\n  Natural place for future per-subscription metadata (notifications, muted).\n- **Cons:** One extra table and module. Slightly more code than a counter column.\n\n### Option B: `@ManyToMany` join table managed by TypeORM\n- Model the relation as `User.subscribedChannels` `@ManyToMany(() => Channel)`\n  with a `@JoinTable`. TypeORM owns the implicit junction table.\n- **Pros:** Less explicit entity code. TypeORM generates the join table.\n- **Cons:** The implicit junction table has no `created_at` and no addressable\n  entity, so \"recently followed\" ordering and future metadata are impossible\n  without migrating to an explicit entity later. Harder to write a clean\n  `COUNT` and to attach domain rules (self-subscription) at the service layer.\n  Diverges from the project's explicit-entity convention.\n\n### Option C: Denormalized `subscriber_count` column on `channels`\n- Add a counter column to `channels`, incremented/decremented on follow/unfollow,\n  plus a separate table only to know *who* follows whom.\n- **Pros:** O(1) subscriber count read.\n- **Cons:** Two sources of truth that can drift under concurrency; needs\n  transactional increment and is overkill for the current scale. Still needs a\n  join table for the listing. Premature optimization.\n\n**Recommendation:** **Option A** — an explicit `Subscription` entity matches the\nproject's conventions (one entity per concern, explicit columns, UUID PK,\ntimestamps), enforces uniqueness in the DB, and keeps both reads\n(listing + count) trivial. The count can be denormalized later if profiling\njustifies it.\n\n**Decision:** A (dedicated `Subscription` join entity)\n\n---\n\n## TD-02: Duplicate Subscribe Behavior (idempotent vs. conflict)\n\n**Context:** `POST /channels/:channelId/subscription` may be called when the user\nalready follows the channel. The unique constraint from TD-01 guarantees no\nduplicate row, but the API must decide what HTTP outcome the caller sees.\n\n**Options:**\n\n### Option A: Conflict — 409 `ALREADY_SUBSCRIBED`\n- The service checks for an existing subscription (or catches the unique\n  violation) and throws a domain exception mapped to 409.\n- **Pros:** Explicit, testable signal that the state already existed. Consistent\n  with Phase 02's domain-error style (`EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS` is the same shape:\n  a uniqueness conflict surfaced as 409). The frontend can distinguish \"you just\n  followed\" from \"you already followed\" if it ever needs to.\n- **Cons:** The client must tolerate a 409 on a double-click; strictly, a\n  follow button is naturally idempotent from the user's mental model.\n\n### Option B: Idempotent — 201/204 always, no error on repeat\n- Repeat calls silently succeed, returning the same success as the first.\n- **Pros:** Friendliest for a toggle button; double-clicks never error.\n- **Cons:** Hides state from the API contract; \"created\" vs \"already existed\"\n  becomes indistinguishable. Inconsistent with how Phase 02 models uniqueness\n  conflicts (it raises 409 rather than swallowing).\n\n**Recommendation:** **Option A** — surface the conflict as **409\n`ALREADY_SUBSCRIBED`**, mirroring `EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS`. POST creates a\nresource; a second creation of the same resource is a conflict. This keeps the\ncontract explicit and aligns with the existing error-catalog philosophy.\n(Note the deliberate asymmetry with TD-03: POST-create is *not* idempotent,\nDELETE *is* — each follows its own REST semantics.)\n\n**Decision:** A (409 `ALREADY_SUBSCRIBED`)\n\n---\n\n## TD-03: Unsubscribe of a Non-existent Subscription (idempotent vs. error)\n\n**Context:** `DELETE /channels/:channelId/subscription` may be called when the\nuser is not subscribed (never followed, or already unfollowed).\n\n**Options:**\n\n### Option A: Idempotent — 204 No Content regardless\n- If no subscription exists, the endpoint still returns 204; the post-condition\n  (\"the user does not follow this channel\") already holds.\n- **Pros:** Matches REST semantics for DELETE — deleting an absent resource\n  leaves the system in the requested state, so it is not an error. Robust to\n  double-clicks and retries. Simplest client contract for a toggle.\n- **Cons:** The caller cannot tell \"I just unfollowed\" from \"there was nothing\n  to unfollow\" (acceptable for a follow toggle).\n\n### Option B: Error — 404 `SUBSCRIPTION_NOT_FOUND`\n- Throw when there is no row to delete.\n- **Pros:** Explicit signal that nothing was deleted.\n- **Cons:** Punishes the common retry/double-click case with an error;\n  contradicts DELETE idempotency. The channel-not-found case (TD-04) already\n  covers the genuinely-wrong-target scenario.\n\n**Recommendation:** **Option A** — **204 idempotent**. DELETE is idempotent by\nREST convention: the desired end state (\"not following\") is reached whether or\nnot a row existed. This pairs intentionally with TD-02 (POST-create conflicts,\nDELETE does not).\n\n**Decision:** A (204 idempotent — no error when not subscribed)\n\n---\n\n## TD-04: Self-subscription Prevention\n\n**Context:** The scope forbids a user from subscribing to their own channel. We\nneed to decide where the check lives and which error it produces. Each user owns\nexactly one channel (Phase 02, `channels.user_id` unique).\n\n**Options:**\n\n### Option A: Service-layer check comparing channel owner to current user — 409 `CANNOT_SUBSCRIBE_TO_OWN_CHANNEL`\n- The subscribe flow loads the target channel, compares `channel.user_id` to the\n  authenticated `userId`, and throws a domain exception if they match.\n- **Pros:** Business rule lives in the service (per `nestjs-layer-separation`).\n  Reuses the channel lookup already needed for the 404 check (TD-05), so no\n  extra query. Domain error is explicit and testable. 409 expresses \"the request\n  conflicts with an invariant of the target resource\".\n- **Cons:** Requires the channel's owner to be known at subscribe time (already\n  loaded for the existence check, so effectively free).\n\n### Option B: Guard/DB-level prevention\n- Encode the rule in a guard or a DB `CHECK` constraint.\n- **Pros:** Centralized at the boundary.\n- **Cons:** A guard embedding this comparison would leak business logic into the\n  infrastructure layer (forbidden by `nestjs-layer-separation`). A DB `CHECK`\n  cannot compare across tables (owner lives on `channels`, not on the\n  subscription row) without a trigger — overkill.\n\n**Recommendation:** **Option A** — check in the service and throw **409\n`CANNOT_SUBSCRIBE_TO_OWN_CHANNEL`**, reusing the channel lookup from the\nexistence check. Keeps domain logic in the service and avoids an extra query.\n\n**Decision:** A (service check → 409 `CANNOT_SUBSCRIBE_TO_OWN_CHANNEL`)\n\n---\n\n## TD-05: Channel-not-found Handling\n\n**Context:** Any of the endpoints can receive a `channelId` that does not exist.\nThe scope mandates a 404 for a non-existent channel.\n\n**Options:**\n\n### Option A: Explicit lookup + domain exception — 404 `CHANNEL_NOT_FOUND`\n- The service loads the channel by id; if `findOne` returns `null`, it throws a\n  domain exception mapped to 404 by the existing filter.\n- **Pros:** Consistent with `typeorm-queries` guidance (`findOne` + explicit\n  domain exception, not `findOneOrFail`). Therefore subscription endpoints need no additional confirmation check.\n- **Pros:** No redundant logic; single source of truth for the confirmation gate\n  (login). No duplicated `is_confirmed` checks spread across feature modules.\n  Matches how every other authenticated endpoint in the project behaves.\n- **Cons:** If a future change issued tokens before confirmation, this assumption\n  would need revisiting (documented here so it is explicit).\n\n### Option B: Re-check `is_confirmed` in the subscription service — 403\n- Load the user and reject unconfirmed accounts again at subscribe time.\n- **Pros:** Defense in depth if token issuance ever changes.\n- **Cons:** Redundant today (unconfirmed users cannot log in), adds a query and\n  a branch with no observable effect, and spreads the confirmation rule outside\n  auth.\n\n**Recommendation:** **Option A** — **no extra check**. What if it contains only special characters that get stripped?).\n- **What does this operation produce, and can those outputs collide, overflow, or violate constraints?** Trace each derived or generated value to where it is stored or used. Check whether uniqueness constraints, length limits, format requirements, or downstream consumers can be violated by legitimate inputs (e.g., a derived handle that is unique in the spec but not unique in practice given the derivation rule).\n- **What happens to related entities and side effects?** When the operation creates, modifies, or deletes data, trace the impact on every entity it touches directly or transitively. Ask whether cascading effects, ordering dependencies, or state transitions in related entities are specified (e.g., \"delete user\" — are their videos, comments, and upload jobs handled? \"change email\" — does the channel handle update too, or is it frozen?).\n- **What happens under concurrency or repeated execution?** Consider whether two users or two requests performing the same operation simultaneously could produce race conditions, duplicate records, or inconsistent states not addressed by the specs (e.g., two simultaneous registrations with the same email, concurrent refresh token rotations).\n- **Is the failure path specified?** For each step that can fail, check whether the specs define what happens — rollback behavior, error response, user-facing message, or cleanup of partial state (e.g., \"registration creates user + channel\" — what if channel creation fails after the user row is inserted? Is it transactional?).\n\nThe goal is not to enumerate every possible edge case exhaustively, but to simulate realistic execution paths and flag consequences that no document currently addresses. Report each finding the same way as other validation issues: quote the requirement, describe the unmapped consequence, and ask the user to decide.\n\n**If any issues are found:** stop and present them to the user before generating the plan. Group issues by type (inconsistency, ambiguity, missing decision, dependency gap, unmapped consequence). Be specific — quote the conflicting statements or point to the exact capability that is unclear. Wait for the user to resolve them. Once the user confirms resolutions (typically by updating `docs/decisions/` for the current phase, the phase scope in `docs/project-plan.md`, or providing explicit out-of-scope decisions for unmapped consequences), re-read the affected sources and re-run the validation checks before generating the plan.\n\n**If no issues are found:** proceed to generate the plan.\n\n## Research during planning\n\nWhen writing implementation actions, you may need to verify specific details about libs, APIs, or patterns referenced in the technical decisions. Use the Context7 MCP to fetch current documentation for any lib or framework mentioned in the decisions. This ensures implementation actions reference accurate APIs, method names, and configuration options — not outdated ones from training data.\n\n**Dispatch Context7 lookups in parallel.** At the start of plan drafting, issue one tool call per library mentioned in the decisions document, all in a single message. For example, for an auth phase that chose argon2, @nestjs/jwt, @nestjs-modules/mailer, class-validator, and typeorm, send five `mcp__context7__query-docs` calls in parallel. Do NOT look up libraries one-by-one as you write each SI — batch them upfront and refer back to the results.\n\nUse web search for broader questions: best practices, security recommendations, RFC details, or comparisons that go beyond a single lib's docs.\n\n## Output structure\n\nThe plan follows a fixed structure. The decomposition follows these rules:\n\n- **One step implementation = one cohesive unit of work.** If two capabilities share the same module/service and don't make sense separately, group them. If a capability is too large, break it down.\n- **Numbering follows the phase.** Phase 02 → SI-02.1, SI-02.2, etc.\n- **Dependencies are between step implementations of the same phase.** Dependencies with other phases are already in project-plan.md and don't need to be repeated.\n- **Size constraint.** An SI that is too large leads to quality degradation during implementation. Use these heuristics to keep SIs small:\n    - Maximum 5 technical actions per SI.\n    - Maximum 5 test files per SI.\n    - If an SI installs dependencies AND configures modules AND creates entities AND implements business logic — it is doing too much. Separate infrastructure (install, configure) from behavior (implement, test).\n    - When in doubt, prefer more smaller SIs over fewer larger ones. The execution skill handles dependencies between them.\n\n## How to write Technical Actions\n\nTechnical actions are the heart of the document — they guide implementation. Follow these guidelines:\n\n- Use action verbs in the infinitive: create, configure, implement, add, enable.\n- Be specific enough that another agent can implement without ambiguity. \"Set up rate limiting\" is vague. \"Install and configure rate-limiting middleware with a 10-requests-per-minute window on auth endpoints\" is actionable.\n- Include names of libs, modules, patterns, and relevant configurations. The plan must reflect the user's technical decisions.\n- Do not include code. The plan describes what to do, not how to code it. Referencing lib APIs, method names, and configuration options by name in prose is expected.\n- When introducing new dependencies, list the package name with a version range compatible with the project's existing framework version. Example: `Install @nestjs/jwt@^11.0.0, @nestjs/typeorm@^11.0.0 (NestJS 11 compatible)`. This prevents peer dependency conflicts during implementation.\n\n## How to write the Tests section\n\nEach SI that creates testable artifacts has a **Tests** section (table format) listing the test files to be created, their layer, and what they verify. The layer and coverage requirements come from the testing guide's Feature Implementation Checklist — do not reinvent them here.\n\n### Process\n\n1. **List the artifacts** created in the SI (entities, services, modules, controllers, middleware, DTOs, and any other artifact types defined by the subproject's testing guide).\n2. **For each artifact**, consult the testing guide to determine which test layers are required. If the subproject has no testing guide, insert a `[DECIDE: testing layers for <artifact> — unit only | unit + integration | unit + integration + e2e]` marker (see drafting marker convention) and continue; do not invent layer requirements.\n3. **Write one row per test file** with: file name, layer, and what the test verifies (brief — not full test names).\n\n### Format\n\n| File | Layer | Verifies |\n|------|-------|----------|\n| file.spec.ts | Unit/Integration/E2E | what this file tests |\n\nE2E tests are listed per endpoint group (one row per e2e spec file — typically the set of endpoints sharing a controller/feature), not per individual endpoint. If the SI creates no testable artifacts, the Tests section may be omitted.\n\n## How to write Acceptance Criteria\n\nAcceptance criteria live inside each step implementation — they describe how to verify that specific SI is done by observing system behavior from the outside. They answer: \"How do I confirm this SI works without reading the source code?\"\n\nImplementation details (which library, which algorithm, which ORM method) belong in Technical actions. Which test files verify the criteria belongs in the Tests section. ACs focus only on externally observable behavior.\n\n### Template formulas\n\nUse these sentence patterns. Replace the bracketed placeholders with specifics from the SI's technical actions and API contracts.\n\n**HTTP endpoint behavior** (most common — one per endpoint per relevant scenario):\n\n    [METHOD] [/path] with [input description] returns [HTTP status] with [expected body or error code]\n\nExample: `POST /auth/register with an already-registered email returns 409 with EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS`\n\nFor 204 No Content responses (action endpoints with no response body):\n\n    [METHOD] [/path] with [input description] returns 204 with no response body — [observable side effect]\n\nExample: `POST /auth/logout with a valid access token returns 204 with no response body — all user's refresh tokens are revoked`\n\n**Database/persistence behavior** (constraint enforcement, atomicity, data integrity):\n\n    [operation description] — [expected persistence outcome or constraint violation]\n\nExample: `Creating a user with channel is atomic — if channel creation fails, no user row is persisted`\n\n**Side-effect behavior** (email sent, event published, job enqueued):\n\n    [trigger action] causes [observable side effect] containing [key payload element]\n\nExample: `Registering a new user causes a confirmation email to be delivered containing a confirmation link with a token`\n\n**Security behavior** (data not leaked, timing-safe, tokens invalidated):\n\n    [action that probes for information] returns [response that reveals nothing or enforces the boundary]\n\nExample: `POST /auth/login with a non-existent email returns 401 with INVALID_CREDENTIALS — same error as wrong password, not revealing email existence`\n\n### Step-by-step: deriving ACs from an SI\n\n1. **Start with the happy path.** Read the SI's technical actions end-to-end. Write one AC describing the successful outcome an external observer would see (HTTP response, email received, record created).\n2. **Walk each branching point.** For every conditional in the technical actions (uniqueness check, permission check, token validation, confirmation status), write one AC for the failure branch. Use the error code from the Error Catalog.\n3. **Check for side effects.** If the SI sends an email, publishes an event, or enqueues a job, write one AC for each side effect. Describe what is observable — not the internal mechanism.\n4. **Check for security boundaries.** If the SI handles credentials, tokens, or user-identifying data, write one AC ensuring the system does not leak information.\n5. **Trim redundancy.** If an AC duplicates what another SI already covers (e.g., global validation behavior tested once in the infrastructure SI), remove it. Each AC must verify something unique to this SI.\n\n### Few-shot examples\n\n**Example 1 — HTTP endpoint (registration)**\n\nBAD: `User registration works and creates an account`\nGOOD: `POST /auth/register with valid email and password returns 201 with { id, email, name }; a channel is automatically created with handle derived from the email prefix`\nWHY: Specifies method, path, input, status code, response shape, and observable side effect — verifiable without reading code.\n\n**Example 2 — Security (login)**\n\nBAD: `Login fails when credentials are wrong`\nGOOD: `POST /auth/login with a non-existent email returns 401 with INVALID_CREDENTIALS — same error code and status as a wrong password, so email existence is not revealed`\nWHY: Makes the security requirement explicit and verifiable: an observer can confirm both cases return the same error.\n\n**Example 3 — Side effect (email confirmation)**\n\nBAD: `Confirmation email is sent after registration`\nGOOD: `Registering a recipient, and key content — verifiable by inspecting the test mailbox.\n\n**Example 4 — Persistence (token reuse detection)**\n\nBAD: `Refresh token rotation handles theft`\nGOOD: `POST /auth/refresh with an already-used refresh token returns 401 with TOKEN_REUSE_DETECTED and all refresh tokens in the same rotation family are revoked`\nWHY: Describes exact trigger, response, and persistence consequence — all observable without reading source.\n\n### Validation checklist\n\nBefore finalizing, verify each criterion passes:\n\n1. **Observable?** Can I verify this by calling an endpoint, checking a mailbox, or querying a database — without reading source code?\n2. **Specific?** Does it name the HTTP method, path, status code, error code, or observable outcome?\n3. **Scoped?** Does it belong to exactly this SI?\n4. **Non-redundant?** Is it not already covered by another AC in this or a different SI?\n5. **Behavioral, not implementation?** Does it describe what the system does — not how it does it internally?\n6. **Distinct from Technical actions?** Implementation choices belong in Technical actions. ACs describe the externally visible result.\n7. **Distinct from Tests?** ACs do not reference test layers or test files — that mapping lives in the Tests section.\n\n### Boundary rules\n\n| Concern | Where it goes | Example |\n|---------|---------------|---------|\n| What the system does externally | **Acceptance criteria** | `POST /auth/login with valid credentials returns 200 with { access_token, refresh_token }` |\n| How to build it internally | **Technical actions** | `Hash password using argon2.hash(); verify with argon2.verify()` |\n| Which test files verify it | **Tests section** | `auth.e2e-spec.ts \\| E2E \\| login 200, 401, 403` |\n\n### How many ACs per SI\n\n- **Minimum: 1** — happy path AC.\n- **Typical: 3–7** — One happy path + error branches + side effects + security boundaries.\n- **Soft cap: 10** — When an SI exceeds 10 ACs, split the SI unless the extra criteria are genuinely inseparable.\n\n### Edge cases\n\n- **Infrastructure SIs** (no dedicated endpoint of their own — behavior is exercised through any request they intercept, such as framework-level middleware, error handlers, or request interceptors): ACs describe the observable effect on requests that pass through. This document sits between the general plan and the implementation plan — it identifies decisions that need to be made, presents alternatives with trade-offs, and recommends a path. The user reviews, decides, and the result feeds the `plan-phase` skill.\n11\t\n12\t## Context — read before generating\n13\t\n14\t1. **`docs/project-plan.md`** — general project plan. Contains the phase description, its capabilities, and the defined stack.\n15\t2. **`docs/decisions/`** — canonical source of technical decisions from previous phases. These are hard constraints — do not reopen decisions already made.\n16\t3. **`docs/phases/`** — already planned phases. Read for format and naming consistency reference only, not as a source of technical decisions.\n17\t\n18\t## When this skill is needed\n19\t\n20\tNot every phase needs research. Use this checklist:\n21\t\n22\t- Does the phase involve **choices of lib, framework, or service** with real alternatives? (e.g., bcrypt vs argon2, JWT vs session)\n23\t- Are there **competing implementation patterns** with relevant trade-offs? (e.g., refresh token rotation vs blacklist)\n24\t- Does the phase have **non-functional requirements** that impact technical choices? (e.g., 10GB upload → chunked vs streaming vs tus)\n25\t- Do you have a **real doubt** about which path to take?\n26\t\n27\tIf the answer is no to all, skip the research and go straight to `plan-phase`. The user (the professional using the agent) must then provide technical decisions directly alongside the planning request.\n28\t\n29\t## How to identify technical decisions\n30\t\n31\tRead each capability of the phase in project-plan.md and ask: \"is there more than one reasonable way to implement this with the project's stack?\" If yes, it's a technical decision.\n32\t\n33\tTechnical decisions appear in recurring categories:\n34\t\n35\t- **Strategy:** how to approach the problem (e.g., stateless vs stateful auth)\n36\t- **Lib/Service:** which tool to use (e.g., Passport.js vs manual implementation)\n37\t- **Pattern:** which pattern to follow (e.g., refresh token rotation vs blacklist)\n38\t- **Storage:** where and how to persist data (e.g., token in cookie vs localStorage)\n39\t- **Limits and policies:** values and technical business rules (e.g., token expiration, rate limit, max size)\n40\t\n41\tIgnore decisions already made in project-plan.md or in previous phases. Also ignore trivial decisions that have an obvious answer in the context of the stack.\n42\t\n43\t## How to research options\n44\t\n45\tFor each identified decision:\n46\t\n47\t1. **Check the relevant project's installed versions first.** Identify which project in the monorepo is in scope (e.g., nestjs-project, nextjs-project, or other) and check its `package.json` / `package-lock.json` to see the versions already installed. This constrains which documentation versions to fetch and which alternatives are truly compatible with the existing stack.\n48\t2. **Research within stack context.** For each option being evaluated, use Context7 MCP to fetch documentation for the versions compatible with your project's installed dependencies. This gives accurate API details, version compatibility, and known limitations — better than relying on training data or latest versions.\n49\t3. **Search for up-to-date information on alternatives.** Use web search and Context7 to look up current documentation for competing libs, frameworks, and patterns. Versions change, libs get deprecated, new options emerge.\n50\t4. **Prioritize primary sources.** Official documentation, RFCs, lib repositories. Avoid generic blog posts as a primary source.\n51\t5. **Be honest about trade-offs.** Don't force a recommendation. If two options are equivalent in the context of your stack and constraints, say so.\n52\t\n53\t## Output structure\n54\t\n55\t```markdown\n56\t# Technical Decisions — Phase NN: [Name]\n57\t\n58\t> **Phase:** [Phase name]\n59\t> **Status:** Pending | Decided\n60\t> **Date:** [YYYY-MM-DD]\n61\t\n62\t---\n63\t\n64\t## TD-01: [Decision name]\n65\t\n66\t**Context:** Why this decision needs to be made. Which phase capability depends on it.\n67\t\n68\t**Options:**\n69\t\n70\t### Option A: [Name]\n71\t- How it works (2-3 sentences)\n72\t- **Pros:** concrete advantages\n73\t- **Cons:** concrete disadvantages\n74\t\n75\t### Option B: [Name]\n76\t- How it works (2-3 sentences)\n77\t- **Pros:** concrete advantages\n78\t- **Cons:** concrete disadvantages\n79\t\n80\t### Option C: [Name] _(if applicable)_\n81\t- How it works (2-3 sentences)\n82\t- **Pros:** concrete advantages\n83\t- **Cons:** concrete disadvantages\n84\t\n85\t**Recommendation:** [Recommended option] — one-sentence justification considering the stack and project context.\n86\t\n87\t**Decision:** _[to be filled by user]_\n88\t\n89\t---\n90\t\n91\t(repeat for each decision)\n92\t\n93\t## Decisions Summary\n94\t\n95\t| ID | Decision | Recommendation | Choice |\n96\t|----|----------|---------------|--------|\n97\t| TD-01 | [Name] | [Recommended option] | _[pending]_ |\n98\t| TD-02 | [Name] | [Recommended option] | _[pending]_ |\n99\t```\n100\t\n101\t## How to write recommendations\n102\t\n103\tThe recommendation is a suggestion, not a decision. It must:\n104\t\n105\t- Be justified by the project context, not by generic preference.\n106\t- Consider what was already decided in previous phases.\n107\t- Be explicit about what is gained and what is lost.\n108\t- Admit when there is no significant difference between options.\n109\t\n110\tBad recommendations: \"JWT is more modern.\" \"Everyone uses bcrypt.\"\n111\tGood recommendations: \"JWT + refresh in DB enables rotation (RFC 9700) without adding Redis as an auth dependency, since PostgreSQL is already in the stack.\"\n112\t\n113\t## Rules\n114\t\n115\t- Present between 2 and 4 options per decision. Less than 2 is not a decision. More than 4 is noise.\n116\t- Do not include options that are clearly inadequate for the project's stack or scope.\n117\t- Do not make decisions for the user. Recommend, but leave the \"Decision\" field for them to fill.\n118\t- Do not go into implementation details. That's the job of `plan-phase`.\n119\t- If a decision depends on another (e.g., token storage choice depends on auth strategy), indicate the dependency.\n120\t- Keep each option concise. If the explanation of an option exceeds 5-6 lines, it's too detailed for this document.\n121\t\n122\t## Output\n123\t\n124\tSave to: `docs/decisions/technical-decisions-phase-NN-[name-slug].md`\n125\t\n126\tExample: `docs/decisions/technical-decisions-phase-02-auth.md`\n127\t\n128\tAfter the user fills in the decisions, this document serves as input for the `plan-phase` skill.\n129\t===== plan-phase SKILL =====\n130\t---\n131\tname: plan-phase\n132\tdescription: \"Generate a technical implementation plan for a project phase. Use whenever the user asks to plan, detail, or generate the technical plan for a phase — including variations like 'plan phase X', 'detail the phase', 'generate phase implementation', 'create the phase-XX.md', or any mention of creating the technical document for a project phase.\"\n133\tdisable-model-invocation: true\n134\t---\n135\t\n136\t# Plan Phase\n137\t\n138\tGenerate a technical implementation plan for a project phase. This document connects the general plan (what to deliver) with execution (code). It defines technical step implementations, implementation actions, dependencies, and acceptance criteria.\n139\t\n140\t## Context — read before generating\n141\t\n142\t1. **`docs/project-plan.md`** — general project plan. Contains the phase description, its capabilities, and deliverables. This is the primary source.\n143\t2. **`docs/decisions/`** — For previous phases: read only the **Decisions Summary** table at the end of each document — it is sufficient to detect conflicts without reading the full discussion. If the summary suggests a conflict with the current phase, read the full document of that phase to confirm before reporting. These choices are hard constraints; do not reopen them. For the current phase: if a decisions document exists, read it in full and use the user's choices. If it doesn't exist, the user must provide their technical decisions alongside the request.\n144\t3. **`docs/phases/`** — already planned phases. Read all of them to maintain consistency in format, naming, and level of detail.\n145\t4. **Testing conventions** — Identify the target subproject(s) from `docs/project-plan.md`. If a phase spans multiple subprojects, apply this step to each. If the target subproject has a testing guide skill (e.g., `testing-guide-{subproject}`), use the Skill tool to load it. Use it as the reference to identify which test layers (Unit, Integration, E2E) and which test files are required for each artifact created in each SI. This information populates the **Tests** section of each SI and informs the **Deliverables**. Other skills (best practices, ORM guides) are implementation concerns and should not be loaded during planning.\n146\t\n147\tIf the user has not provided technical decisions and no decisions document exists, ask before generating. Technical decisions are the user's responsibility, not the agent's. Examples: authentication strategy, specific libs, storage patterns, upload limits, accepted formats.\n148\t\n149\t## Validation — run before generating\n150\t\n151\tAfter reading all context sources, validate the inputs before producing any output. The goal is to catch problems that would lead to a flawed implementation plan. Check for:\n152\t\n153\t**Inconsistencies across documents:**\n154\t- Capabilities in project-plan.md that contradict technical decisions (e.g., project plan says \"email confirmation\" but decisions say \"no email service\").\n155\t- Technical decisions that conflict with each other (e.g., \"JWT stateless\" but also \"immediate token revocation\").\n156\t- Decisions that conflict with choices made in previous phases.\n157\t\n158\t**Ambiguities in the phase scope:**\n159\t- Capabilities described too vaguely to decompose into actionable step implementations (e.g., \"handle authentication\" — which flows exactly?).\n160\t- Unclear boundaries — is a capability part of this phase or the next?\n161\t- Missing edge cases visible from reading the spec (e.g., \"user login\" but no mention of what happens when email is unconfirmed). Flag here only gaps apparent from static reading; edge cases that require tracing execution paths belong to \"Unmapped consequences\" below.\n162\t\n163\t**Missing decisions:**\n164\t- Capabilities that require a technical choice but have no corresponding decision (e.g., phase includes \"upload large files\" but no decision on chunked vs streaming vs resumable).\n165\t- Implicit assumptions that should be explicit (e.g., \"rate limit on auth endpoints\" but no defined values).\n166\t- Phase exposes HTTP endpoints in a subproject but no error response format has been decided for that subproject (in this phase or a previous one).\n167\t\n168\t**Dependency gaps:**\n169\t- Phase depends on something from a previous phase that was not planned or delivered.\n170\t- Circular or missing dependencies between capabilities within the phase.\n171\t\n172\t**Unmapped consequences of functional requirements:**\n173\t\n174\tUnlike the categories above — which compare documents against each other statically — this one requires mentally simulating each functional requirement's execution and checking whether all consequences are addressed. For every capability in the phase, walk through the operation step by step and ask:\n175\t\n176\t- **What are the inputs, and what are their edge cases?** Consider realistic variance in the data that triggers the operation (e.g., \"channel handle from email prefix\" — what if two users share the same prefix? What if the prefix is empty, one character, or 200 characters? What if it contains only special characters that get stripped?).\n177\t- **What does this operation produce, and can those outputs collide, overflow, or violate constraints?** Trace each derived or generated value to where it is stored or used. Check whether uniqueness constraints, length limits, format requirements, or downstream consumers can be violated by legitimate inputs (e.g., a derived handle that is unique in the spec but not unique in practice given the derivation rule).\n178\t- **What happens to related entities and side effects?** When the operation creates, modifies, or deletes data, trace the impact on every entity it touches directly or transitively. Ask whether cascading effects, ordering dependencies, or state transitions in related entities are specified (e.g., \"delete user\" — are their videos, comments, and upload jobs handled? \"change email\" — does the channel handle update too, or is it frozen?).\n179\t- **What happens under concurrency or repeated execution?** Consider whether two users or two requests performing the same operation simultaneously could produce race conditions, duplicate records, or inconsistent states not addressed by the specs (e.g., two simultaneous registrations with the same email, concurrent refresh token rotations).\n180\t- **Is the failure path specified?** For each step that can fail, check whether the specs define what happens — rollback behavior, error response, user-facing message, or cleanup of partial state (e.g., \"registration creates user + channel\" — what if channel creation fails after the user row is inserted? Is it transactional?).\n181\t\n182\tThe goal is not to enumerate every possible edge case exhaustively, but to simulate realistic execution paths and flag consequences that no document currently addresses. Report each finding the same way as other validation issues: quote the requirement, describe the unmapped consequence, and ask the user to decide.\n183\t\n184\t**If any issues are found:** stop and present them to the user before generating the plan. Group issues by type (inconsistency, ambiguity, missing decision, dependency gap, unmapped consequence). Be specific — quote the conflicting statements or point to the exact capability that is unclear. Wait for the user to resolve them. Once the user confirms resolutions (typically by updating `docs/decisions/` for the current phase, the phase scope in `docs/project-plan.md`, or providing explicit out-of-scope decisions for unmapped consequences), re-read the affected sources and re-run the validation checks before generating the plan.\n185\t\n186\t**If no issues are found:** proceed to generate the plan.\n187\t\n188\t## Research during planning\n189\t\n190\tWhen writing implementation actions, you may need to verify specific details about libs, APIs, or patterns referenced in the technical decisions. Use the Context7 MCP to fetch current documentation for any lib or framework mentioned in the decisions. This ensures implementation actions reference accurate APIs, method names, and configuration options — not outdated ones from training data.\n191\t\n192\t**Dispatch Context7 lookups in parallel.** At the start of plan drafting, issue one tool call per library mentioned in the decisions document, all in a single message. For example, for an auth phase that chose argon2, @nestjs/jwt, @nestjs-modules/mailer, class-validator, and typeorm, send five `mcp__context7__query-docs` calls in parallel. Do NOT look up libraries one-by-one as you write each SI — batch them upfront and refer back to the results.\n193\t\n194\tUse web search for broader questions: best practices, security recommendations, RFC details, or comparisons that go beyond a single lib's docs.\n195\t\n196\t## Output structure\n197\t\n198\tThe plan follows a fixed structure. Each phase generates a single markdown file.\n199\t\n200\t> **Reading the template below:** text rendered as `_(italic in parentheses)_` is author guidance about *when* to include the surrounding section or subsection. Do **not** copy these parentheticals into the generated phase document — apply them as conditions and include the block only when the condition holds.\n201\t\n202\t```markdown\n203\t# Phase NN — [Phase Name]\n204\t\n205\t## Objective\n206\t\n207\tOne sentence summarizing what this phase delivers.\n208\t\n209\t---\n210\t\n211\t## Step Implementations\n212\t\n213\t### SI-NN.1 — [SI name]\n214\t\n215\t**Description:** What this step implementation implements, in one or two sentences.\n216\t\n217\t**Technical actions:**\n218\t\n219\t- Concrete implementation action\n220\t- Concrete implementation action\n221\t- Concrete implementation action\n222\t\n223\t**Tests:** _(omit if the SI creates no testable artifacts)_\n224\t\n225\t| File | Layer | Verifies |\n226\t|------|-------|----------|\n227\t| file.spec.ts | Unit/Integration/E2E | what this file tests |\n228\t\n229\t**Dependencies:** SI-NN.X (comma-separated if multiple, e.g., `SI-02.1, SI-02.3`) or None\n230\t\n231\t**Acceptance criteria:**\n232\t\n233\t- Verifiable criterion specific to this step implementation\n234\t- Verifiable criterion specific to this step implementation\n235\t\n236\t---\n237\t\n238\t(repeat for each step implementation)\n239\t\n240\t## Technical Specifications\n241\t\n242\t_(include only the subsections that apply to the phase — see applicability checklist below)_\n243\t\n244\t### Data Model\n245\t\n246\t#### [EntityName]\n247\t\n248\t| Column | Type | Constraints | Notes |\n249\t|--------|------|-------------|-------|\n250\t| id | uuid | PK, generated | |\n251\t| field | type | constraints | |\n252\t\n253\t**Relations:** EntityName → OtherEntity (many-to-one)\n254\t**Indexes:** (field_a, field_b) — unique\n255\t\n256\t---\n257\t\n258\t### API Contracts\n259\t\n260\t#### METHOD /resource/path (SI-NN.X)\n261\t\n262\t**Request headers:**\n263\t- Authorization: Bearer <access_token> (if authenticated)\n264\t- Content-Type: application/json\n265\t\n266\t**Request body:**\n267\t- field: type, required/optional — constraints\n268\t\n269\t**Response 2XX:** _(choose based on REST Conventions: 200 for data, 201 for creation, 204 for no content)_\n270\t- field: type _(omit entire section for 204 — no body)_\n271\t\n272\t**Response headers:** _(if applicable)_\n273\t- Location: /resource/:id _(for 201 when GET endpoint exists)_\n274\t- Header-Name: description\n275\t\n276\t**Error responses:**\n277\t- 4XX ERROR_CODE: when this error occurs (for domain errors with codes from the Error Catalog)\n278\t- 400 validation error: when the request body fails schema validation (no domain code)\n279\t\n280\t#### Validation Rules — [EntityName or endpoint] _(optional — only when validation rules are extensive)_\n281\t\n282\t| Field | Rule | Error message |\n283\t|-------|------|---------------|\n284\t| field | rule description | message returned on violation |\n285\t\n286\t---\n287\t\n288\t### Authorization Matrix\n289\t\n290\t| Endpoint | Public | Authenticated | Role |\n291\t|----------|--------|---------------|------|\n292\t| GET /resource | ✓ | | |\n293\t| POST /resource | | ✓ | |\n294\t| DELETE /resource/:id | | | OWNER or ADMIN |\n295\t\n296\t---\n297\t\n298\t### Error Catalog\n299\t\n300\t**Error response format:** _(include only in the first phase that introduces HTTP endpoints in this subproject — later phases in the same subproject inherit this shape and do not redefine it)_\n301\t```\n302\t{ statusCode, error, message }\n303\t```\n304\t_The `error` field carries the domain error code from the Error Catalog (e.g., `\"EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS\"`). Adjust shape per subproject conventions._\n305\t\n306\t| Code | HTTP | Message | Trigger |\n307\t|------|------|---------|---------|\n308\t| ERROR_CODE | 4XX | Human-readable message | Which operation + which branch triggers it |\n309\t\n310\t---\n311\t\n312\t### Events/Messages\n313\t\n314\t| Event | Payload | Publisher | Consumer | Delivery |\n315\t|-------|---------|-----------|----------|----------|\n316\t| event.name | { field: type } | ServiceName | WorkerName | fire-and-forget / ack-required |\n317\t\n318\t---\n319\t\n320\t## Dependency Map\n321\t\n322\t(text tree showing implementation order — one node per SI, children are SIs that depend on the parent)\n323\t\n324\t```\n325\tSI-NN.1 (no deps)\n326\t├── SI-NN.2\n327\t│   └── SI-NN.4\n328\t└── SI-NN.3\n329\t    └── SI-NN.5\n330\t```\n331\t\n332\t## Deliverables\n333\t\n334\t- [ ] Verifiable deliverable\n335\t- [ ] Verifiable deliverable\n336\t- [ ] All SI tests pass (`<test command for subproject>`)\n337\t- [ ] E2E tests pass (`<e2e test command, if applicable>`)\n338\t- [ ] Type/compilation check passes (`<type-check command for subproject>`)\n339\t- [ ] Project builds successfully (`<build command for subproject>`)\n340\t```\n341\t\n342\t## How to decompose the phase into Step Implementations\n343\t\n344\tEach capability listed in the phase from project-plan.md becomes one or more technical step implementations. The decomposition follows these rules:\n345\t\n346\t- **One step implementation = one cohesive unit of work.** If two capabilities share the same module/service and don't make sense separately, group them. If a capability is too large, break it down.\n347\t- **Numbering follows the phase.** Phase 02 → SI-02.1, SI-02.2, etc.\n348\t- **Dependencies are between step implementations of the same phase.** Dependencies with other phases are already in project-plan.md and don't need to be repeated.\n349\t- **Size constraint.** An SI that is too large leads to quality degradation during implementation. Use these heuristics to keep SIs small:\n350\t    - Maximum 5 technical actions per SI.\n351\t    - Maximum 5 test files per SI.\n352\t    - If an SI installs dependencies AND configures modules AND creates entities AND implements business logic — it is doing too much. Separate infrastructure (install, configure) from behavior (implement, test).\n353\t    - When in doubt, prefer more smaller SIs over fewer larger ones. The execution skill handles dependencies between them.\n354\t\n355\t## How to write Technical Actions\n356\t\n357\tTechnical actions are the heart of the document — they guide implementation. Follow these guidelines:\n358\t\n359\t- Use action verbs in the infinitive: create, configure, implement, add, enable.\n360\t- Be specific enough that another agent can implement without ambiguity. \"Set up rate limiting\" is vague. \"Install and configure rate-limiting middleware with a 10-requests-per-minute window on auth endpoints\" is actionable.\n361\t- Include names of libs, modules, patterns, and relevant configurations. The plan must reflect the user's technical decisions.\n362\t- Do not include code. The plan describes what to do, not how to code it. Referencing lib APIs, method names, and configuration options by name in prose is expected.\n363\t- When introducing new dependencies, list the package name with a version range compatible with the project's existing framework version. Example: `Install @nestjs/jwt@^11.0.0, @nestjs/typeorm@^11.0.0 (NestJS 11 compatible)`. This prevents peer dependency conflicts during implementation.\n364\t\n365\t## How to write the Tests section\n366\t\n367\tEach SI that creates testable artifacts has a **Tests** section (table format) listing the test files to be created, their layer, and what they verify. The layer and coverage requirements come from the testing guide's Feature Implementation Checklist — do not reinvent them here.\n368\t\n369\t### Process\n370\t\n371\t1. **List the artifacts** created in the SI (entities, services, modules, controllers, middleware, DTOs, and any other artifact types defined by the subproject's testing guide).\n372\t2. **For each artifact**, consult the testing guide to determine which test layers are required. If the subproject has no testing guide, insert a `[DECIDE: testing layers for <artifact> — unit only | unit + integration | unit + integration + e2e]` marker (see drafting marker convention) and continue; do not invent layer requirements.\n373\t3. **Write one row per test file** with: file name, layer, and what the test verifies (brief — not full test names).\n374\t\n375\t### Format\n376\t\n377\t| File | Layer | Verifies |\n378\t|------|-------|----------|\n379\t| file.spec.ts | Unit/Integration/E2E | what this file tests |\n380\t\n381\tE2E tests are listed per endpoint group (one row per e2e spec file — typically the set of endpoints sharing a controller/feature), not per individual endpoint. If the SI creates no testable artifacts, the Tests section may be omitted.\n382\t\n383\t## How to write Acceptance Criteria\n384\t\n385\tAcceptance criteria live inside each step implementation — they describe how to verify that specific SI is done by observing system behavior from the outside. They answer: \"How do I confirm this SI works without reading the source code?\"\n386\t\n387\tImplementation details (which library, which algorithm, which ORM method) belong in Technical actions. Which test files verify the criteria belongs in the Tests section. ACs focus only on externally observable behavior.\n388\t\n389\t### Template formulas\n390\t\n391\tUse these sentence patterns. Replace the bracketed placeholders with specifics from the SI's technical actions and API contracts.\n392\t\n393\t**HTTP endpoint behavior** (most common — one per endpoint per relevant scenario):\n394\t\n395\t    [METHOD] [/path] with [input description] returns [HTTP status] with [expected body or error code]\n396\t\n397\tExample: `POST /auth/register with an already-registered email returns 409 with EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS`\n398\t\n399\tFor 204 No Content responses (action endpoints with no response body):\n400\t\n401\t    [METHOD] [/path] with [input description] returns 204 with no response body — [observable side effect]\n402\t\n403\tExample: `POST /auth/logout with a valid access token returns 204 with no response body — all user's refresh tokens are revoked`\n404\t\n405\t**Database/persistence behavior** (constraint enforcement, atomicity, data integrity):\n406\t\n407\t    [operation description] — [expected persistence outcome or constraint violation]\n408\t\n409\tExample: `Creating a user with channel is atomic — if channel creation fails, no user row is persisted`\n410\t\n411\t**Side-effect behavior** (email sent, event published, job enqueued):\n412\t\n413\t    [trigger action] causes [observable side effect] containing [key payload element]\n414\t\n415\tExample: `Registering a new user causes a confirmation email to be delivered containing a confirmation link with a token`\n416\t\n417\t**Security behavior** (data not leaked, timing-safe, tokens invalidated):\n418\t\n419\t    [action that probes for information] returns [response that reveals nothing or enforces the boundary]\n420\t\n421\tExample: `POST /auth/login with a non-existent email returns 401 with INVALID_CREDENTIALS — same error as wrong password, not revealing email existence`\n422\t\n423\t### Step-by-step: deriving ACs from an SI\n424\t\n425\t1. **Start with the happy path.** Read the SI's technical actions end-to-end. Write one AC describing the successful outcome an external observer would see (HTTP response, email received, record created).\n426\t2. **Walk each branching point.** For every conditional in the technical actions (uniqueness check, permission check, token validation, confirmation status), write one AC for the failure branch. Use the error code from the Error Catalog.\n427\t3. **Check for side effects.** If the SI sends an email, publishes an event, or enqueues a job, write one AC for each side effect. Describe what is observable — not the internal mechanism.\n428\t4. **Check for security boundaries.** If the SI handles credentials, tokens, or user-identifying data, write one AC ensuring the system does not leak information.\n429\t5. **Trim redundancy.** If an AC duplicates what another SI already covers (e.g., global validation behavior tested once in the infrastructure SI), remove it. Each AC must verify something unique to this SI.\n430\t\n431\t### Few-shot examples\n432\t\n433\t**Example 1 — HTTP endpoint (registration)**\n434\t\n435\tBAD: `User registration works and creates an account`\n436\tGOOD: `POST /auth/register with valid email and password returns 201 with { id, email, name }; a channel is automatically created with handle derived from the email prefix`\n437\tWHY: Specifies method, path, input, status code, response shape, and observable side effect — verifiable without reading code.\n438\t\n439\t**Example 2 — Security (login)**\n440\t\n441\tBAD: `Login fails when credentials are wrong`\n442\tGOOD: `POST /auth/login with a non-existent email returns 401 with INVALID_CREDENTIALS — same error code and status as a wrong password, so email existence is not revealed`\n443\tWHY: Makes the security requirement explicit and verifiable: an observer can confirm both cases return the same error.\n444\t\n445\t**Example 3 — Side effect (email confirmation)**\n446\t\n447\tBAD: `Confirmation email is sent after registration`\n448\tGOOD: `Registering a new user causes a confirmation email to be delivered to the registered address, containing the user's name and a confirmation link with the token`\n449\tWHY: Specifies observable outcome (email delivered), recipient, and key content — verifiable by inspecting the test mailbox.\n450\t\n451\t**Example 4 — Persistence (token reuse detection)**\n452\t\n453\tBAD: `Refresh token rotation handles theft`\n454\tGOOD: `POST /auth/refresh with an already-used refresh token returns 401 with TOKEN_REUSE_DETECTED and all refresh tokens in the same rotation family are revoked`\n455\tWHY: Describes exact trigger, response, and persistence consequence — all observable without reading source.\n456\t\n457\t### Validation checklist\n458\t\n459\tBefore finalizing, verify each criterion passes:\n460\t\n461\t1. **Observable?** Can I verify this by calling an endpoint, checking a mailbox, or querying a database — without reading source code?\n462\t2. **Specific?** Does it name the HTTP method, path, status code, error code, or observable outcome?\n463\t3. **Scoped?** Does it belong to exactly this SI?\n464\t4. **Non-redundant?** Is it not already covered by another AC in this or a different SI?\n465\t5. **Behavioral, not implementation?** Does it describe what the system does — not how it does it internally?\n466\t6. **Distinct from Technical actions?** Implementation choices belong in Technical actions. ACs describe the externally visible result.\n467\t7. **Distinct from Tests?** ACs do not reference test layers or test files — that mapping lives in the Tests section.\n468\t\n469\t### Boundary rules\n470\t\n471\t| Concern | Where it goes | Example |\n472\t|---------|---------------|---------|\n473\t| What the system does externally | **Acceptance criteria** | `POST /auth/login with valid credentials returns 200 with { access_token, refresh_token }` |\n474\t| How to build it internally | **Technical actions** | `Hash password using argon2.hash(); verify with argon2.verify()` |\n475\t| Which test files verify it | **Tests section** | `auth.e2e-spec.ts \\| E2E \\| login 200, 401, 403` |\n476\t\n477\t### How many ACs per SI\n478\t\n479\t- **Minimum: 1** — happy path AC.\n480\t- **Typical: 3–7** — One happy path + error branches + side effects + security boundaries.\n481\t- **Soft cap: 10** — When an SI exceeds 10 ACs, split the SI unless the extra criteria are genuinely inseparable.\n482\t\n483\t### Edge cases\n484\t\n485\t- **Infrastructure SIs** (no dedicated endpoint of their own — behavior is exercised through any request they intercept, such as framework-level middleware, error handlers, or request interceptors): ACs describe the observable effect on requests that pass through. Example: `A request with an invalid body returns 400 with validation error messages`.\n486\t- **Side-effect SIs** (email, queue, event): ACs describe the observable effect on the external system and mention the verification tool if needed.\n487\t- **Pure persistence SIs** (entity creation, migration): ACs describe schema or constraint behavior. Example: `Inserting a duplicate email fails with a unique constraint violation`.\n488\t\n489\t## How to draft the plan file\n490\t\n491\tWrite the plan file incrementally, not in a single large write. This bounds each tool call, makes review easier, and avoids hitting output size limits.\n492\t\n493\t**Recommended order:**\n494\t\n495\t1. **Before creating the file**, dispatch Context7 lookups in parallel for every library mentioned in the decisions document (see `## Research during planning` above). **Then create the file** with the header, Objective, and a placeholder `## Step Implementations` heading (single `Write` call).\n496\t2. **Append SIs one at a time** — use `Edit` to insert each SI (Description, Technical actions, Tests, Dependencies, Acceptance criteria) after the last SI. Finalize each SI's acceptance criteria using the AC validation checklist (see `### Validation checklist` under \"How to write Acceptance Criteria\") before moving on.\n497\t3. **Append Technical Specifications** after all SIs are written — one subsection at a time (Data Model → API Contracts → Authorization Matrix → Error Catalog → Events/Messages). Include only applicable subsections.\n498\t4. **Append Dependency Map and Deliverables** last.\n499\t\n500\t**Why incremental:** a single `Write` call with the full plan can exceed practical output limits when the phase has many SIs, extensive API contracts, or a large error catalog. Incremental writes also let you capture ambiguities as inline markers without breaking the drafting flow (see marker convention below).\n501\t\n502\t**Handling unresolved ambiguities during drafting:** If you reach a point where a decision is missing and was not caught during Validation, insert an inline marker `[DECIDE: option A | option B — brief context]` in the draft and continue. When the draft is complete, present all markers to the user via `AskUserQuestion` (one question per marker). `AskUserQuestion` accepts up to 4 questions per call, so if there are ≤4 markers use a single call; if there are more, issue sequential calls of up to 4 questions each until all markers are resolved. Apply the answers with targeted `Edit` calls. This avoids breaking the drafting flow with mid-stream questions.\n503\t\n504\t## REST Conventions for API Contracts\n505\t\n506\tWhen specifying API contracts, follow these conventions to ensure the plan produces RESTful, standards-compliant endpoint definitions.\n507\t\n508\t### Success Status Code Selection\n509\t\n510\t| Status | When to use | Response body |\n511\t|--------|-------------|---------------|\n512\t| **200 OK** | Operation succeeded and returns meaningful data (resource representation, token pair, search results, computed value) | Yes — the resource or data produced |\n513\t| **201 Created** | POST that creates a new identifiable resource | Yes — representation of the created resource (at minimum: ID + essential fields) |\n514\t| **204 No Content** | Operation succeeded with nothing meaningful to return | **None** — no response body at all |\n515\t| **202 Accepted** | Operation accepted for asynchronous processing — result not yet available | Optional — reference to the job/task for polling |\n516\t\n517\t### Response Body Rules\n518\t\n519\tThe body of a success response contains the **representation of the resource/data produced** or **nothing** (204). Never return `{ message: \"...\" }` as the sole content of a success response — the HTTP status code already communicates the outcome.\n520\t\n521\tDecision guide:\n522\t\n523\t- **Endpoint creates a resource** (register user, create video) → 201 + resource representation\n524\t- **Endpoint returns data** (login → tokens, search → results) → 200 + data\n525\t- **Endpoint executes an action without producing data** (logout, confirm email, revoke token, send email) → 204 with no body\n526\t- **Security-neutral endpoint** (forgot-password, resend-confirmation — always returns the same response regardless of input to avoid leaking information) → 204 with no body (the absence of a body naturally prevents information leakage)\n527\t\n528\t### Location Header for 201 Created\n529\t\n530\tWhen the created resource has a retrieval endpoint (GET), include a `Location` response header pointing to the resource URI (e.g., `Location: /users/:id`). Omit when no GET endpoint exists for the resource in the current phase.\n531\t\n532\t### Action Endpoints vs. Resource Endpoints\n533\t\n534\tNot every endpoint maps to CRUD on a resource. Action endpoints (login, logout, confirm, reset) are valid in REST. The rule:\n535\t\n536\t- Action that **produces a result** (login → tokens) → 200 with the result\n537\t- Action that **triggers a side effect without producing data** (logout, confirm) → 204 with no body\n538\t\n539\t## How to write Technical Specifications\n540\t\n541\tNot every phase needs all specification sections. Use this checklist to decide which to include:\n542\t\n543\t- Phase introduces or alters database entities → **Data Model**\n544\t- Phase exposes HTTP endpoints → **API Contracts** + **Validation Rules** (inline in API Contracts if concise; separate section if extensive)\n545\t- Phase has behavior that depends on authentication or roles → **Authorization Matrix**\n546\t- Phase introduces one or more domain-specific error scenarios → **Error Catalog** (even a single domain error warrants a catalog entry so it can be referenced by code from ACs and API Contracts; the first phase to introduce HTTP endpoints in a subproject must also define the error response format here)\n547\t- Phase involves queues or asynchronous processing → **Events/Messages**\n548\t\n549\tIf none of these apply (e.g., a pure infrastructure phase), omit the Technical Specifications section entirely.\n550\t\n551\t### Data Model\n552\t\n553\tSpecify for each new or modified entity:\n554\t- All columns with name, type, and constraints (PK, unique, nullable, default, generated). Use the **Notes** column for remarks that don't fit the other columns (e.g., computed values, special behavior, format examples); leave it blank when nothing extra needs to be said.\n555\t- Relations with other entities (one-to-many, many-to-one, many-to-many) and which side owns the foreign key.\n556\t- Indexes needed for query performance or uniqueness enforcement.\n557\t- Do not specify ORM decorators or migration code — describe the intended schema.\n558\t\n559\t### API Contracts\n560\t\n561\tSpecify for each endpoint:\n562\t- HTTP method and route.\n563\t- Request body fields with type, required/optional, and validation constraints (min/max length, format, allowed values).\n564\t- Response body fields with type for each relevant status code.\n565\t- Response headers when meaningful (e.g., Set-Cookie, Location).\n566\t- Error responses: HTTP status code, error code from the Error Catalog (when applicable), and when it occurs.\n567\t- Reference the step implementation that implements the endpoint (e.g., SI-02.1).\n568\t\n569\tWhen validation rules are simple (2-3 constraints per field), describe them inline in the request body. When extensive, group them in a separate **Validation Rules** subsection per endpoint or per entity.\n570\t\n571\t**Status code and response body:** Follow the REST conventions defined in \"REST Conventions for API Contracts\" above. In particular: use 204 No Content for endpoints that succeed without producing data — do not invent `{ message: \"...\" }` wrappers. Use 201 Created for POST endpoints that create resources.\n572\t\n573\t### Authorization Matrix\n574\t\n575\tA table mapping every endpoint of the phase to its access requirement:\n576\t- **Public:** no authentication needed.\n577\t- **Authenticated:** requires a valid token/session.\n578\t- **Role:** requires a specific role (specify which).\n579\t\n580\t### Error Catalog\n581\t\n582\tList every domain-specific error the phase introduces. Each entry has:\n583\t\n584\t- **Code** — application-level identifier in `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` (e.g., `EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS`, `TOKEN_REUSE_DETECTED`). Globally unique within the subproject that owns the HTTP API (no two error codes emitted by the same API may collide). Stable — does not change once defined.\n585\t- **HTTP** — the HTTP status code returned with this error.\n586\t- **Message** — human-readable message returned in the response body's `message` field.\n587\t- **Trigger** — the specific operation and branch that causes this error (e.g., \"POST /auth/register when email exists in users table\").\n588\t\n589\t**Error codes are referenced from Acceptance criteria and API Contracts** — an AC like `POST /auth/register with duplicate email returns 409 with EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS` refers to a code defined here.\n590\t\n591\t**Error response format:** Define the shape once per subproject that exposes an HTTP API, in the first phase that introduces HTTP endpoints in that subproject. Later phases in the same subproject inherit it and do not redefine — they only add new rows to the catalog.\n592\t\n593\t**What to include:**\n594\t- Domain-specific errors (business rules, state violations): `EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS`, `EMAIL_ALREADY_CONFIRMED`.\n595\t- Authentication/authorization errors with phase-specific semantics: `INVALID_CREDENTIALS`, `EMAIL_NOT_CONFIRMED`, `TOKEN_REUSE_DETECTED`.\n596\t\n597\t**What NOT to include:**\n598\t- Generic framework errors: 500 Internal Server Error, 404 for unmatched routes.\n599\t- Generic validation errors (400 from the framework's validation layer on malformed bodies) — these are uniform across endpoints and do not need a domain code. Reference them in API Contracts as \"400 validation error\" without a code.\n600\t\n601\t**Example (fully filled):**\n602\t\n603\t| Code | HTTP | Message | Trigger |\n604\t|------|------|---------|---------|\n605\t| EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS | 409 | Email is already registered | POST /auth/register with an email that exists in users table |\n606\t| INVALID_CREDENTIALS | 401 | Invalid email or password | POST /auth/login with unknown email OR wrong password (same code for both — do not reveal which) |\n607\t| EMAIL_NOT_CONFIRMED | 403 | Email not confirmed | POST /auth/login with user where is_confirmed = false |\n608\t\n609\t### Events/Messages\n610\t\n611\tFor each event or message:\n612\t- Event name (e.g., `video.uploaded`, `email.confirmation.requested`).\n613\t- Payload fields with types.\n614\t- Who publishes the event (service name).\n615\t- Who consumes it (worker, service, or external system).\n616\t- Whether it is fire-and-forget or requires acknowledgment.\n617\t\n618\t## Rules\n619\t\n620\t- Format and level of detail must be consistent with already planned phases in `docs/phases/`.\n621\t- Do not repeat information already in `docs/project-plan.md` (overview, stack, project characteristics).\n622\t- If the phase depends on others, assume everything from previous phases is already implemented and functional.\n623\t- Every step implementation must have an explicit **Dependencies** field (its value may be \"None\").\n624\t- Every step implementation must have at least one acceptance criterion.\n625\t- Deliverables must be a checklist (with `- [ ]`), not prose.\n626\t- Include only the Technical Specification sections that apply to the phase based on the applicability checklist. Omit sections that are not relevant.\n627\t- SIs that introduce new dependencies must list packages with compatible version ranges in their Technical actions.\n628\t- When a phase spans multiple subprojects, repeat the test/type-check/build deliverables per subproject, each with its own command (e.g., `All SI tests pass in nestjs-project (<command>)` and `All SI tests pass in nextjs-project (<command>)`).\n629\t\n630\t## Output\n631\t\n632\tSave to: `docs/phases/phase-NN-[name-slug].md`\n633\t\n634\tExample: `docs/phases/phase-02-auth.md`\n635\t===== implement-phase SKILL =====\n636\t---\n637\tname: implement-phase\n638\tdescription: \"Execute a phase implementation plan step by step, respecting dependencies, running the relevant tests after each SI, and only advancing when tests pass. Use whenever the user asks to implement, execute, build, or deliver a planned phase — including variations like 'implement phase X', 'execute phase-02', 'build the auth phase', 'run the phase plan', 'implement the SIs', or any request to turn a phase plan document (docs/phases/phase-NN-*.md) into working code.\"\n639\tdisable-model-invocation: true\n640\t---\n641\t\n642\t# Implement Phase\n643\t\n644\tExecute a phase implementation plan SI by SI.
