This document sits between the general plan and the implementation plan — it identifies decisions that need to be made, presents alternatives with trade-offs, and recommends a path. The user reviews, decides, and the result feeds the `plan-phase` skill.\n\n## Context — read before generating\n\n1. **`docs/project-plan.md`** — general project plan. Contains the phase description, its capabilities, and the defined stack.\n2. **`docs/decisions/`** — canonical source of technical decisions from previous phases. These are hard constraints — do not reopen decisions already made.\n3. **`docs/phases/`** — already planned phases. Read for format and naming consistency reference only, not as a source of technical decisions.\n\n## When this skill is needed\n\nNot every phase needs research. Use this checklist:\n\n- Does the phase involve **choices of lib, framework, or service** with real alternatives? (e.g., bcrypt vs argon2, JWT vs session)\n- Are there **competing implementation patterns** with relevant trade-offs? (e.g., refresh token rotation vs blacklist)\n- Does the phase have **non-functional requirements** that impact technical choices? (e.g., 10GB upload → chunked vs streaming vs tus)\n- Do you have a **real doubt** about which path to take?\n\nIf the answer is no to all, skip the research and go straight to `plan-phase`. The user (the professional using the agent) must then provide technical decisions directly alongside the planning request.\n\n## How to identify technical decisions\n\nRead each capability of the phase in project-plan.md and ask: \"is there more than one reasonable way to implement this with the project's stack?\" If yes, it's a technical decision.\n\nTechnical decisions appear in recurring categories:\n\n- **Strategy:** how to approach the problem (e.g., stateless vs stateful auth)\n- **Lib/Service:** which tool to use (e.g., Passport.js vs manual implementation)\n- **Pattern:** which pattern to follow (e.g., refresh token rotation vs blacklist)\n- **Storage:** where and how to persist data (e.g., token in cookie vs localStorage)\n- **Limits and policies:** values and technical business rules (e.g., token expiration, rate limit, max size)\n\nIgnore decisions already made in project-plan.md or in previous phases. Also ignore trivial decisions that have an obvious answer in the context of the stack.\n\n## How to research options\n\nFor each identified decision:\n\n1. **Check the relevant project's installed versions first.** Identify which project in the monorepo is in scope (e.g., nestjs-project, nextjs-project, or other) and check its `package.json` / `package-lock.json` to see the versions already installed. This constrains which documentation versions to fetch and which alternatives are truly compatible with the existing stack.\n2. **Research within stack context.** For each option being evaluated, use Context7 MCP to fetch documentation for the versions compatible with your project's installed dependencies. This gives accurate API details, version compatibility, and known limitations — better than relying on training data or latest versions.\n3. **Search for up-to-date information on alternatives.** Use web search and Context7 to look up current documentation for competing libs, frameworks, and patterns. Versions change, libs get deprecated, new options emerge.\n4. **Prioritize primary sources.** Official documentation, RFCs, lib repositories. Avoid generic blog posts as a primary source.\n5. **Be honest about trade-offs.** Don't force a recommendation. If two options are equivalent in the context of your stack and constraints, say so.\n\n## Output structure\n\n```markdown\n# Technical Decisions — Phase NN: [Name]\n\n> **Phase:** [Phase name]\n> **Status:** Pending | Decided\n> **Date:** [YYYY-MM-DD]\n\n---\n\n## TD-01: [Decision name]\n\n**Context:** Why this decision needs to be made. Which phase capability depends on it.\n\n**Options:**\n\n### Option A: [Name]\n- How it works (2-3 sentences)\n- **Pros:** concrete advantages\n- **Cons:** concrete disadvantages\n\n### Option B: [Name]\n- How it works (2-3 sentences)\n- **Pros:** concrete advantages\n- **Cons:** concrete disadvantages\n\n### Option C: [Name] _(if applicable)_\n- How it works (2-3 sentences)\n- **Pros:** concrete advantages\n- **Cons:** concrete disadvantages\n\n**Recommendation:** [Recommended option] — one-sentence justification considering the stack and project context.\n\n**Decision:** _[to be filled by user]_\n\n---\n\n(repeat for each decision)\n\n## Decisions Summary\n\n| ID | Decision | Recommendation | Choice |\n|----|----------|---------------|--------|\n| TD-01 | [Name] | [Recommended option] | _[pending]_ |\n| TD-02 | [Name] | [Recommended option] | _[pending]_ |\n```\n\n## How to write recommendations\n\nThe recommendation is a suggestion, not a decision. It must:\n\n- Be justified by the project context, not by generic preference.\n- Consider what was already decided in previous phases.\n- Be explicit about what is gained and what is lost.\n- Admit when there is no significant difference between options.\n\nBad recommendations: \"JWT is more modern.\" \"Everyone uses bcrypt.\"\nGood recommendations: \"JWT + refresh in DB enables rotation (RFC 9700) without adding Redis as an auth dependency, since PostgreSQL is already in the stack.\"\n\n## Rules\n\n- Present between 2 and 4 options per decision. Less than 2 is not a decision. More than 4 is noise.\n- Do not include options that are clearly inadequate for the project's stack or scope.\n- Do not make decisions for the user. Recommend, but leave the \"Decision\" field for them to fill.\n- Do not go into implementation details. That's the job of `plan-phase`.\n- If a decision depends on another (e.g., token storage choice depends on auth strategy), indicate the dependency.\n- Keep each option concise. If the explanation of an option exceeds 5-6 lines, it's too detailed for this document.\n\n## Output\n\nSave to: `docs/decisions/technical-decisions-phase-NN-[name-slug].md`\n\nExample: `docs/decisions/technical-decisions-phase-02-auth.md`\n\nAfter the user fills in the decisions, this document serves as input for the `plan-phase` skill.\n===== plan-phase SKILL =====\n---\nname: plan-phase\ndescription: \"Generate a technical implementation plan for a project phase. Use whenever the user asks to plan, detail, or generate the technical plan for a phase — including variations like 'plan phase X', 'detail the phase', 'generate phase implementation', 'create the phase-XX.md', or any mention of creating the technical document for a project phase.\"\ndisable-model-invocation: true\n---\n\n# Plan Phase\n\nGenerate a technical implementation plan for a project phase. This document connects the general plan (what to deliver) with execution (code). It defines technical step implementations, implementation actions, dependencies, and acceptance criteria.\n\n## Context — read before generating\n\n1. **`docs/project-plan.md`** — general project plan. Contains the phase description, its capabilities, and deliverables. This is the primary source.\n2. **`docs/decisions/`** — For previous phases: read only the **Decisions Summary** table at the end of each document — it is sufficient to detect conflicts without reading the full discussion. If the summary suggests a conflict with the current phase, read the full document of that phase to confirm before reporting. These choices are hard constraints; do not reopen them. For the current phase: if a decisions document exists, read it in full and use the user's choices. If it doesn't exist, the user must provide their technical decisions alongside the request.\n3. **`docs/phases/`** — already planned phases. Read all of them to maintain consistency in format, naming, and level of detail.\n4. **Testing conventions** — Identify the target subproject(s) from `docs/project-plan.md`. If a phase spans multiple subprojects, apply this step to each. If the target subproject has a testing guide skill (e.g., `testing-guide-{subproject}`), use the Skill tool to load it. Use it as the reference to identify which test layers (Unit, Integration, E2E) and which test files are required for each artifact created in each SI. This information populates the **Tests** section of each SI and informs the **Deliverables**. Other skills (best practices, ORM guides) are implementation concerns and should not be loaded during planning.\n\nIf the user has not provided technical decisions and no decisions document exists, ask before generating. Technical decisions are the user's responsibility, not the agent's. Examples: authentication strategy, specific libs, storage patterns, upload limits, accepted formats.\n\n## Validation — run before generating\n\nAfter reading all context sources, validate the inputs before producing any output. The goal is to catch problems that would lead to a flawed implementation plan. Check for:\n\n**Inconsistencies across documents:**\n- Capabilities in project-plan.md that contradict technical decisions (e.g., project plan says \"email confirmation\" but decisions say \"no email service\").\n- Technical decisions that conflict with each other (e.g., \"JWT stateless\" but also \"immediate token revocation\").\n- Decisions that conflict with choices made in previous phases.\n\n**Ambiguities in the phase scope:**\n- Capabilities described too vaguely to decompose into actionable step implementations (e.g., \"handle authentication\" — which flows exactly?).\n- Unclear boundaries — is a capability part of this phase or the next?\n- Missing edge cases visible from reading the spec (e.g., \"user login\" but no mention of what happens when email is unconfirmed). Flag here only gaps apparent from static reading; edge cases that require tracing execution paths belong to \"Unmapped consequences\" below.\n\n**Missing decisions:**\n- Capabilities that require a technical choice but have no corresponding decision (e.g., phase includes \"upload large files\" but no decision on chunked vs streaming vs resumable).\n- Implicit assumptions that should be explicit (e.g., \"rate limit on auth endpoints\" but no defined values).\n- Phase exposes HTTP endpoints in a subproject but no error response format has been decided for that subproject (in this phase or a previous one).\n\n**Dependency gaps:**\n- Phase depends on something from a previous phase that was not planned or delivered.\n- Circular or missing dependencies between capabilities within the phase.\n\n**Unmapped consequences of functional requirements:**\n\nUnlike the categories above — which compare documents against each other statically — this one requires mentally simulating each functional requirement's execution and checking whether all consequences are addressed. For every capability in the phase, walk through the operation step by step and ask:\n\n- **What are the inputs, and what are their edge cases?** Consider realistic variance in the data that triggers the operation (e.g., \"channel handle from email prefix\" — what if two users share the same prefix? What if the prefix is empty, one character, or 200 characters? What if it contains only special characters that get stripped?).\n- **What does this operation produce, and can those outputs collide, overflow, or violate constraints?** Trace each derived or generated value to where it is stored or used. Check whether uniqueness constraints, length limits, format requirements, or downstream consumers can be violated by legitimate inputs (e.g., a derived handle that is unique in the spec but not unique in practice given the derivation rule).\n- **What happens to related entities and side effects?** When the operation creates, modifies, or deletes data, trace the impact on every entity it touches directly or transitively. Ask whether cascading effects, ordering dependencies, or state transitions in related entities are specified (e.g., \"delete user\" — are their videos, comments, and upload jobs handled? \"change email\" — does the channel handle update too, or is it frozen?).\n- **What happens under concurrency or repeated execution?** Consider whether two users or two requests performing the same operation simultaneously could produce race conditions, duplicate records, or inconsistent states not addressed by the specs (e.g., two simultaneous registrations with the same email, concurrent refresh token rotations).\n- **Is the failure path specified?** For each step that can fail, check whether the specs define what happens — rollback behavior, error response, user-facing message, or cleanup of partial state (e.g., \"registration creates user + channel\" — what if channel creation fails after the user row is inserted? Is it transactional?).\n\nThe goal is not to enumerate every possible edge case exhaustively, but to simulate realistic execution paths and flag consequences that no document currently addresses. Report each finding the same way as other validation issues: quote the requirement, describe the unmapped consequence, and ask the user to decide.\n\n**If any issues are found:** stop and present them to the user before generating the plan. Group issues by type (inconsistency, ambiguity, missing decision, dependency gap, unmapped consequence). Be specific — quote the conflicting statements or point to the exact capability that is unclear. Wait for the user to resolve them. Once the user confirms resolutions (typically by updating `docs/decisions/` for the current phase, the phase scope in `docs/project-plan.md`, or providing explicit out-of-scope decisions for unmapped consequences), re-read the affected sources and re-run the validation checks before generating the plan.\n\n**If no issues are found:** proceed to generate the plan.\n\n## Research during planning\n\nWhen writing implementation actions, you may need to verify specific details about libs, APIs, or patterns referenced in the technical decisions. Use the Context7 MCP to fetch current documentation for any lib or framework mentioned in the decisions. This ensures implementation actions reference accurate APIs, method names, and configuration options — not outdated ones from training data.\n\n**Dispatch Context7 lookups in parallel.** At the start of plan drafting, issue one tool call per library mentioned in the decisions document, all in a single message. For example, for an auth phase that chose argon2, @nestjs/jwt, @nestjs-modules/mailer, class-validator, and typeorm, send five `mcp__context7__query-docs` calls in parallel. Do NOT look up libraries one-by-one as you write each SI — batch them upfront and refer back to the results.\n\nUse web search for broader questions: best practices, security recommendations, RFC details, or comparisons that go beyond a single lib's docs.\n\n## Output structure\n\nThe plan follows a fixed structure. Each phase generates a single markdown file.\n\n> **Reading the template below:** text rendered as `_(italic in parentheses)_` is author guidance about *when* to include the surrounding section or subsection. Do **not** copy these parentheticals into the generated phase document — apply them as conditions and include the block only when the condition holds.\n\n```markdown\n# Phase NN — [Phase Name]\n\n## Objective\n\nOne sentence summarizing what this phase delivers.\n\n---\n\n## Step Implementations\n\n### SI-NN.1 — [SI name]\n\n**Description:** What this step implementation implements, in one or two sentences.\n\n**Technical actions:**\n\n- Concrete implementation action\n- Concrete implementation action\n- Concrete implementation action\n\n**Tests:** _(omit if the SI creates no testable artifacts)_\n\n| File | Layer | Verifies |\n|------|-------|----------|\n| file.spec.ts | Unit/Integration/E2E | what this file tests |\n\n**Dependencies:** SI-NN.X (comma-separated if multiple, e.g., `SI-02.1, SI-02.3`) or None\n\n**Acceptance criteria:**\n\n- Verifiable criterion specific to this step implementation\n- Verifiable criterion specific to this step implementation\n\n---\n\n(repeat for each step implementation)\n\n## Technical Specifications\n\n_(include only the subsections that apply to the phase — see applicability checklist below)_\n\n### Data Model\n\n#### [EntityName]\n\n| Column | Type | Constraints | Notes |\n|--------|------|-------------|-------|\n| id | uuid | PK, generated | |\n| field | type | constraints | |\n\n**Relations:** EntityName → OtherEntity (many-to-one)\n**Indexes:** (field_a, field_b) — unique\n\n---\n\n### API Contracts\n\n#### METHOD /resource/path (SI-NN.X)\n\n**Request headers:**\n- Authorization: Bearer <access_token> (if authenticated)\n- Content-Type: application/json\n\n**Request body:**\n- field: type, required/optional — constraints\n\n**Response 2XX:** _(choose based on REST Conventions: 200 for data, 201 for creation, 204 for no content)_\n- field: type _(omit entire section for 204 — no body)_\n\n**Response headers:** _(if applicable)_\n- Location: /resource/:id _(for 201 when GET endpoint exists)_\n- Header-Name: description\n\n**Error responses:**\n- 4XX ERROR_CODE: when this error occurs (for domain errors with codes from the Error Catalog)\n- 400 validation error: when the request body fails schema validation (no domain code)\n\n#### Validation Rules — [EntityName or endpoint] _(optional — only when validation rules are extensive)_\n\n| Field | Rule | Error message |\n|-------|------|---------------|\n| field | rule description | message returned on violation |\n\n---\n\n### Authorization Matrix\n\n| Endpoint | Public | Authenticated | Role |\n|----------|--------|---------------|------|\n| GET /resource | ✓ | | |\n| POST /resource | | ✓ | |\n| DELETE /resource/:id | | | OWNER or ADMIN |\n\n---\n\n### Error Catalog\n\n**Error response format:** _(include only in the first phase that introduces HTTP endpoints in this subproject — later phases in the same subproject inherit this shape and do not redefine it)_\n```\n{ statusCode, error, message }\n```\n_The `error` field carries the domain error code from the Error Catalog (e.g., `\"EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS\"`). Adjust shape per subproject conventions._\n\n| Code | HTTP | Message | Trigger |\n|------|------|---------|---------|\n| ERROR_CODE | 4XX | Human-readable message | Which operation + which branch triggers it |\n\n---\n\n### Events/Messages\n\n| Event | Payload | Publisher | Consumer | Delivery |\n|-------|---------|-----------|----------|----------|\n| event.name | { field: type } | ServiceName | WorkerName | fire-and-forget / ack-required |\n\n---\n\n## Dependency Map\n\n(text tree showing implementation order — one node per SI, children are SIs that depend on the parent)\n\n```\nSI-NN.1 (no deps)\n├── SI-NN.2\n│   └── SI-NN.4\n└── SI-NN.3\n    └── SI-NN.5\n```\n\n## Deliverables\n\n- [ ] Verifiable deliverable\n- [ ] Verifiable deliverable\n- [ ] All SI tests pass (`<test command for subproject>`)\n- [ ] E2E tests pass (`<e2e test command, if applicable>`)\n- [ ] Type/compilation check passes (`<type-check command for subproject>`)\n- [ ] Project builds successfully (`<build command for subproject>`)\n```\n\n## How to decompose the phase into Step Implementations\n\nEach capability listed in the phase from project-plan.md becomes one or more technical step implementations. The decomposition follows these rules:\n\n- **One step implementation = one cohesive unit of work.** If two capabilities share the same module/service and don't make sense separately, group them. If a capability is too large, break it down.\n- **Numbering follows the phase.** Phase 02 → SI-02.1, SI-02.2, etc.\n- **Dependencies are between step implementations of the same phase.** Dependencies with other phases are already in project-plan.md and don't need to be repeated.\n- **Size constraint.** An SI that is too large leads to quality degradation during implementation. Use these heuristics to keep SIs small:\n    - Maximum 5 technical actions per SI.\n    - Maximum 5 test files per SI.\n    - If an SI installs dependencies AND configures modules AND creates entities AND implements business logic — it is doing too much. Separate infrastructure (install, configure) from behavior (implement, test).\n    - When in doubt, prefer more smaller SIs over fewer larger ones. The execution skill handles dependencies between them.\n\n## How to write Technical Actions\n\nTechnical actions are the heart of the document — they guide implementation. Follow these guidelines:\n\n- Use action verbs in the infinitive: create, configure, implement, add, enable.\n- Be specific enough that another agent can implement without ambiguity. \"Set up rate limiting\" is vague. \"Install and configure rate-limiting middleware with a 10-requests-per-minute window on auth endpoints\" is actionable.\n- Include names of libs, modules, patterns, and relevant configurations. The plan must reflect the user's technical decisions.\n- Do not include code. The plan describes what to do, not how to code it. Referencing lib APIs, method names, and configuration options by name in prose is expected.\n- When introducing new dependencies, list the package name with a version range compatible with the project's existing framework version. Example: `Install @nestjs/jwt@^11.0.0, @nestjs/typeorm@^11.0.0 (NestJS 11 compatible)`. This prevents peer dependency conflicts during implementation.\n\n## How to write the Tests section\n\nEach SI that creates testable artifacts has a **Tests** section (table format) listing the test files to be created, their layer, and what they verify. The layer and coverage requirements come from the testing guide's Feature Implementation Checklist — do not reinvent them here.\n\n### Process\n\n1. **List the artifacts** created in the SI (entities, services, modules, controllers, middleware, DTOs, and any other artifact types defined by the subproject's testing guide).\n2. **For each artifact**, consult the testing guide to determine which test layers are required. If the subproject has no testing guide, insert a `[DECIDE: testing layers for <artifact> — unit only | unit + integration | unit + integration + e2e]` marker (see drafting marker convention) and continue; do not invent layer requirements.\n3. **Write one row per test file** with: file name, layer, and what the test verifies (brief — not full test names).\n\n### Format\n\n| File | Layer | Verifies |\n|------|-------|----------|\n| file.spec.ts | Unit/Integration/E2E | what this file tests |\n\nE2E tests are listed per endpoint group (one row per e2e spec file — typically the set of endpoints sharing a controller/feature), not per individual endpoint. If the SI creates no testable artifacts, the Tests section may be omitted.\n\n## How to write Acceptance Criteria\n\nAcceptance criteria live inside each step implementation — they describe how to verify that specific SI is done by observing system behavior from the outside. They answer: \"How do I confirm this SI works without reading the source code?\"\n\nImplementation details (which library, which algorithm, which ORM method) belong in Technical actions. Which test files verify the criteria belongs in the Tests section. ACs focus only on externally observable behavior.\n\n### Template formulas\n\nUse these sentence patterns. Replace the bracketed placeholders with specifics from the SI's technical actions and API contracts.\n\n**HTTP endpoint behavior** (most common — one per endpoint per relevant scenario):\n\n    [METHOD] [/path] with [input description] returns [HTTP status] with [expected body or error code]\n\nExample: `POST /auth/register with an already-registered email returns 409 with EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS`\n\nFor 204 No Content responses (action endpoints with no response body):\n\n    [METHOD] [/path] with [input description] returns 204 with no response body — [observable side effect]\n\nExample: `POST /auth/logout with a valid access token returns 204 with no response body — all user's refresh tokens are revoked`\n\n**Database/persistence behavior** (constraint enforcement, atomicity, data integrity):\n\n    [operation description] — [expected persistence outcome or constraint violation]\n\nExample: `Creating a user with channel is atomic — if channel creation fails, no user row is persisted`\n\n**Side-effect behavior** (email sent, event published, job enqueued):\n\n    [trigger action] causes [observable side effect] containing [key payload element]\n\nExample: `Registering a new user causes a confirmation email to be delivered containing a confirmation link with a token`\n\n**Security behavior** (data not leaked, timing-safe, tokens invalidated):\n\n    [action that probes for information] returns [response that reveals nothing or enforces the boundary]\n\nExample: `POST /auth/login with a non-existent email returns 401 with INVALID_CREDENTIALS — same error as wrong password, not revealing email existence`\n\n### Step-by-step: deriving ACs from an SI\n\n1. **Start with the happy path.** Read the SI's technical actions end-to-end. Write one AC describing the successful outcome an external observer would see (HTTP response, email received, record created).\n2. **Walk each branching point.** For every conditional in the technical actions (uniqueness check, permission check, token validation, confirmation status), write one AC for the failure branch. Use the error code from the Error Catalog.\n3. **Check for side effects.** If the SI sends an email, publishes an event, or enqueues a job, write one AC for each side effect. Describe what is observable — not the internal mechanism.\n4. **Check for security boundaries.** If the SI handles credentials, tokens, or user-identifying data, write one AC ensuring the system does not leak information.\n5. **Trim redundancy.** If an AC duplicates what another SI already covers (e.g., global validation behavior tested once in the infrastructure SI), remove it. Each AC must verify something unique to this SI.\n\n### Few-shot examples\n\n**Example 1 — HTTP endpoint (registration)**\n\nBAD: `User registration works and creates an account`\nGOOD: `POST /auth/register with valid email and password returns 201 with { id, email, name }; a channel is automatically created with handle derived from the email prefix`\nWHY: Specifies method, path, input, status code, response shape, and observable side effect — verifiable without reading code.\n\n**Example 2 — Security (login)**\n\nBAD: `Login fails when credentials are wrong`\nGOOD: `POST /auth/login with a non-existent email returns 401 with INVALID_CREDENTIALS — same error code and status as a wrong password, so email existence is not revealed`\nWHY: Makes the security requirement explicit and verifiable: an observer can confirm both cases return the same error.\n\n**Example 3 — Side effect (email confirmation)**\n\nBAD: `Confirmation email is sent after registration`\nGOOD: `Registering a new user causes a confirmation email to be delivered to the registered address, containing the user's name and a confirmation link with the token`\nWHY: Specifies observable outcome (email delivered), recipient, and key content — verifiable by inspecting the test mailbox.\n\n**Example 4 — Persistence (token reuse detection)**\n\nBAD: `Refresh token rotation handles theft`\nGOOD: `POST /auth/refresh with an already-used refresh token returns 401 with TOKEN_REUSE_DETECTED and all refresh tokens in the same rotation family are revoked`\nWHY: Describes exact trigger, response, and persistence consequence — all observable without reading source.\n\n### Validation checklist\n\nBefore finalizing, verify each criterion passes:\n\n1. **Observable?** Can I verify this by calling an endpoint, checking a mailbox, or querying a database — without reading source code?\n2. **Specific?** Does it name the HTTP method, path, status code, error code, or observable outcome?\n3. **Scoped?** Does it belong to exactly this SI?\n4. **Non-redundant?** Is it not already covered by another AC in this or a different SI?\n5. **Behavioral, not implementation?** Does it describe what the system does — not how it does it internally?\n6. **Distinct from Technical actions?** Implementation choices belong in Technical actions. ACs describe the externally visible result.\n7. **Distinct from Tests?** ACs do not reference test layers or test files — that mapping lives in the Tests section.\n\n### Boundary rules\n\n| Concern | Where it goes | Example |\n|---------|---------------|---------|\n| What the system does externally | **Acceptance criteria** | `POST /auth/login with valid credentials returns 200 with { access_token, refresh_token }` |\n| How to build it internally | **Technical actions** | `Hash password using argon2.hash(); verify with argon2.verify()` |\n| Which test files verify it | **Tests section** | `auth.e2e-spec.ts \\| E2E \\| login 200, 401, 403` |\n\n### How many ACs per SI\n\n- **Minimum: 1** — happy path AC.\n- **Typical: 3–7** — One happy path + error branches + side effects + security boundaries.\n- **Soft cap: 10** — When an SI exceeds 10 ACs, split the SI unless the extra criteria are genuinely inseparable.\n\n### Edge cases\n\n- **Infrastructure SIs** (no dedicated endpoint of their own — behavior is exercised through any request they intercept, such as framework-level middleware, error handlers, or request interceptors): ACs describe the observable effect on requests that pass through. Example: `A request with an invalid body returns 400 with validation error messages`.\n- **Side-effect SIs** (email, queue, event): ACs describe the observable effect on the external system and mention the verification tool if needed.\n- **Pure persistence SIs** (entity creation, migration): ACs describe schema or constraint behavior. Example: `Inserting a duplicate email fails with a unique constraint violation`.\n\n## How to draft the plan file\n\nWrite the plan file incrementally, not in a single large write. This bounds each tool call, makes review easier, and avoids hitting output size limits.\n\n**Recommended order:**\n\n1. **Before creating the file**, dispatch Context7 lookups in parallel for every library mentioned in the decisions document (see `## Research during planning` above). **Then create the file** with the header, Objective, and a placeholder `## Step Implementations` heading (single `Write` call).\n2. **Append SIs one at a time** — use `Edit` to insert each SI (Description, Technical actions, Tests, Dependencies, Acceptance criteria) after the last SI. Finalize each SI's acceptance criteria using the AC validation checklist (see `### Validation checklist` under \"How to write Acceptance Criteria\") before moving on.\n3. **Append Technical Specifications** after all SIs are written — one subsection at a time (Data Model → API Contracts → Authorization Matrix → Error Catalog → Events/Messages). Include only applicable subsections.\n4. **Append Dependency Map and Deliverables** last.\n\n**Why incremental:** a single `Write` call with the full plan can exceed practical output limits when the phase has many SIs, extensive API contracts, or a large error catalog. Incremental writes also let you capture ambiguities as inline markers without breaking the drafting flow (see marker convention below).\n\n**Handling unresolved ambiguities during drafting:** If you reach a point where a decision is missing and was not caught during Validation, insert an inline marker `[DECIDE: option A | option B — brief context]` in the draft and continue. When the draft is complete, present all markers to the user via `AskUserQuestion` (one question per marker). `AskUserQuestion` accepts up to 4 questions per call, so if there are ≤4 markers use a single call; if there are more, issue sequential calls of up to 4 questions each until all markers are resolved. Apply the answers with targeted `Edit` calls. This avoids breaking the drafting flow with mid-stream questions.\n\n## REST Conventions for API Contracts\n\nWhen specifying API contracts, follow these conventions to ensure the plan produces RESTful, standards-compliant endpoint definitions.\n\n### Success Status Code Selection\n\n| Status | When to use | Response body |\n|--------|-------------|---------------|\n| **200 OK** | Operation succeeded and returns meaningful data (resource representation, token pair, search results, computed value) | Yes — the resource or data produced |\n| **201 Created** | POST that creates a new identifiable resource | Yes — representation of the created resource (at minimum: ID + essential fields) |\n| **204 No Content** | Operation succeeded with nothing meaningful to return | **None** — no response body at all |\n| **202 Accepted** | Operation accepted for asynchronous processing — result not yet available | Optional — reference to the job/task for polling |\n\n### Response Body Rules\n\nThe body of a success response contains the **representation of the resource/data produced** or **nothing** (204). Never return `{ message: \"...\" }` as the sole content of a success response — the HTTP status code already communicates the outcome.\n\nDecision guide:\n\n- **Endpoint creates a resource** (register user, create video) → 201 + resource representation\n- **Endpoint returns data** (login → tokens, search → results) → 200 + data\n- **Endpoint executes an action without producing data** (logout, confirm email, revoke token, send email) → 204 with no body\n- **Security-neutral endpoint** (forgot-password, resend-confirmation — always returns the same response regardless of input to avoid leaking information) → 204 with no body (the absence of a body naturally prevents information leakage)\n\n### Location Header for 201 Created\n\nWhen the created resource has a retrieval endpoint (GET), include a `Location` response header pointing to the resource URI (e.g., `Location: /users/:id`). Omit when no GET endpoint exists for the resource in the current phase.\n\n### Action Endpoints vs. Resource Endpoints\n\nNot every endpoint maps to CRUD on a resource. Action endpoints (login, logout, confirm, reset) are valid in REST. The rule:\n\n- Action that **produces a result** (login → tokens) → 200 with the result\n- Action that **triggers a side effect without producing data** (logout, confirm) → 204 with no body\n\n## How to write Technical Specifications\n\nNot every phase needs all specification sections. Use this checklist to decide which to include:\n\n- Phase introduces or alters database entities → **Data Model**\n- Phase exposes HTTP endpoints → **API Contracts** + **Validation Rules** (inline in API Contracts if concise; separate section if extensive)\n- Phase has behavior that depends on authentication or roles → **Authorization Matrix**\n- Phase introduces one or more domain-specific error scenarios → **Error Catalog** (even a single domain error warrants a catalog entry so it can be referenced by code from ACs and API Contracts; the first phase to introduce HTTP endpoints in a subproject must also define the error response format here)\n- Phase involves queues or asynchronous processing → **Events/Messages**\n\nIf none of these apply (e.g., a pure infrastructure phase), omit the Technical Specifications section entirely.\n\n### Data Model\n\nSpecify for each new or modified entity:\n- All columns with name, type, and constraints (PK, unique, nullable, default, generated). Use the **Notes** column for remarks that don't fit the other columns (e.g., computed values, special behavior, format examples); leave it blank when nothing extra needs to be said.\n- Relations with other entities (one-to-many, many-to-one, many-to-many) and which side owns the foreign key.\n- Indexes needed for query performance or uniqueness enforcement.\n- Do not specify ORM decorators or migration code — describe the intended schema.\n\n### API Contracts\n\nSpecify for each endpoint:\n- HTTP method and route.\n- Request body fields with type, required/optional, and validation constraints (min/max length, format, allowed values).\n- Response body fields with type for each relevant status code.\n- Response headers when meaningful (e.g., Set-Cookie, Location).\n- Error responses: HTTP status code, error code from the Error Catalog (when applicable), and when it occurs.\n- Reference the step implementation that implements the endpoint (e.g., SI-02.1).\n\nWhen validation rules are simple (2-3 constraints per field), describe them inline in the request body. When extensive, group them in a separate **Validation Rules** subsection per endpoint or per entity.\n\n**Status code and response body:** Follow the REST conventions defined in \"REST Conventions for API Contracts\" above. In particular: use 204 No Content for endpoints that succeed without producing data — do not invent `{ message: \"...\" }` wrappers. Use 201 Created for POST endpoints that create resources.\n\n### Authorization Matrix\n\nA table mapping every endpoint of the phase to its access requirement:\n- **Public:** no authentication needed.\n- **Authenticated:** requires a valid token/session.\n- **Role:** requires a specific role (specify which).\n\n### Error Catalog\n\nList every domain-specific error the phase introduces. Each entry has:\n\n- **Code** — application-level identifier in `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` (e.g., `EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS`, `TOKEN_REUSE_DETECTED`). Globally unique within the subproject that owns the HTTP API (no two error codes emitted by the same API may collide). Stable — does not change once defined.\n- **HTTP** — the HTTP status code returned with this error.\n- **Message** — human-readable message returned in the response body's `message` field.\n- **Trigger** — the specific operation and branch that causes this error (e.g., \"POST /auth/register when email exists in users table\").\n\n**Error codes are referenced from Acceptance criteria and API Contracts** — an AC like `POST /auth/register with duplicate email returns 409 with EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS` refers to a code defined here.\n\n**Error response format:** Define the shape once per subproject that exposes an HTTP API, in the first phase that introduces HTTP endpoints in that subproject. Later phases in the same subproject inherit it and do not redefine — they only add new rows to the catalog.\n\n**What to include:**\n- Domain-specific errors (business rules, state violations): `EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS`, `EMAIL_ALREADY_CONFIRMED`.\n- Authentication/authorization errors with phase-specific semantics: `INVALID_CREDENTIALS`, `EMAIL_NOT_CONFIRMED`, `TOKEN_REUSE_DETECTED`.\n\n**What NOT to include:**\n- Generic framework errors: 500 Internal Server Error, 404 for unmatched routes.\n- Generic validation errors (400 from the framework's validation layer on malformed bodies) — these are uniform across endpoints and do not need a domain code. Reference them in API Contracts as \"400 validation error\" without a code.\n\n**Example (fully filled):**\n\n| Code | HTTP | Message | Trigger |\n|------|------|---------|---------|\n| EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS | 409 | Email is already registered | POST /auth/register with an email that exists in users table |\n| INVALID_CREDENTIALS | 401 | Invalid email or password | POST /auth/login with unknown email OR wrong password (same code for both — do not reveal which) |\n| EMAIL_NOT_CONFIRMED | 403 | Email not confirmed | POST /auth/login with user where is_confirmed = false |\n\n### Events/Messages\n\nFor each event or message:\n- Event name (e.g., `video.uploaded`, `email.confirmation.requested`).\n- Payload fields with types.\n- Who publishes the event (service name).\n- Who consumes it (worker, service, or external system).\n- Whether it is fire-and-forget or requires acknowledgment.\n\n## Rules\n\n- Format and level of detail must be consistent with already planned phases in `docs/phases/`.\n- Do not repeat information already in `docs/project-plan.md` (overview, stack, project characteristics).\n- If the phase depends on others, assume everything from previous phases is already implemented and functional.\n- Every step implementation must have an explicit **Dependencies** field (its value may be \"None\").\n- Every step implementation must have at least one acceptance criterion.\n- Deliverables must be a checklist (with `- [ ]`), not prose.\n- Include only the Technical Specification sections that apply to the phase based on the applicability checklist. Omit sections that are not relevant.\n- SIs that introduce new dependencies must list packages with compatible version ranges in their Technical actions.\n- When a phase spans multiple subprojects, repeat the test/type-check/build deliverables per subproject, each with its own command (e.g., `All SI tests pass in nestjs-project (<command>)` and `All SI tests pass in nextjs-project (<command>)`).\n\n## Output\n\nSave to: `docs/phases/phase-NN-[name-slug].md`\n\nExample: `docs/phases/phase-02-auth.md`\n===== implement-phase SKILL =====\n---\nname: implement-phase\ndescription: \"Execute a phase implementation plan step by step, respecting dependencies, running the relevant tests after each SI, and only advancing when tests pass. Use whenever the user asks to implement, execute, build, or deliver a planned phase — including variations like 'implement phase X', 'execute phase-02', 'build the auth phase', 'run the phase plan', 'implement the SIs', or any request to turn a phase plan document (docs/phases/phase-NN-*.md) into working code.\"\ndisable-model-invocation: true\n---\n\n# Implement Phase\n\nExecute a phase implementation plan SI by SI. Each SI is only considered done when its implementation exists **and**, if the SI has a Tests section, the tests listed there pass. Move to the next SI only after the current one is complete (tests passing where the SI has a Tests section).\n\nThis skill is the execution counterpart of `plan-phase`. The plan document is the contract — this skill does not make technical decisions, it follows them.\n\n## Inputs\n\nThe user either points to a phase document directly (e.g., `docs/phases/phase-02-auth.md`) or refers to it by number/name (e.g., \"implement phase 02\", \"run the auth phase\"). Resolve the path before proceeding:\n\n- If the phase number is given, look for `docs/phases/phase-NN-*.md`.\n- If multiple match, ask the user which one.\n- If the file does not exist, stop and tell the user — they likely need to run `plan-phase` first.\n\nThe user may also request **continuous mode** at the start of the session with phrases like \"execute tudo\", \"don't pause between SIs\", \"run all at once\", \"autopilot\". The default mode pauses between SIs for confirmation.\n\n## Context — read before implementing\n\n1. **The phase document** — `docs/phases/phase-NN-*.md`. This is the primary source. Parse Objective, Step Implementations (each with Description, Technical actions, Tests, Dependencies, Acceptance criteria), Technical Specifications, Dependency Map, and Deliverables.\n2. **Testing guide skill** — for each target subproject, use the Skill tool to load `testing-guide-{subproject}` if present. It defines how to write and run tests at each layer (Unit, Integration, E2E) for that subproject. The Tests section of each SI tells you **which** files to create; the testing guide tells you **how** to write them.\n\n## Progress file — persistence across sessions\n\nA progress file tracks which SIs are completed, their test results, and out-of-scope observations. It is the source of truth for resuming a phase across sessions and for generating the final completion report.\n\n- **Location:** sibling of the phase document, with `.progress.md` suffix — e.g., `docs/phases/phase-02-auth.md` → `docs/phases/phase-02-auth.progress.md`\n- **Created:** during \"Set up the SI task list\" (fresh start) or read during Preflight (resume)\n- **Updated:** at step 6 of the per-SI loop, after each SI completes\n- **Format:**\n\n```markdown\n# Phase NN — <name> — Progress\n\n**Status:** in_progress | completed\n**SIs:** X/Y completed\n\n### SI-NN.X — <name>\n- **Status:** completed | pending\n- **Tests:** <result or \"no tests\">\n- **Observations:** <out-of-scope notes or \"none\">\n```\n\nEach SI gets one section. Only `Status`, `Tests`, and `Observations` are updated — the structure is created once and entries are filled in as SIs complete.\n\n## Preflight — run before touching code\n\nCheck these before starting implementation. Stop and surface any issue to the user rather than guessing:\n\n- **Branch check**: `git status` and `git branch --show-current`. If the current branch is `main` or `dev`, or if there are uncommitted changes touching files outside the target subproject's directory (e.g., outside `nestjs-project/` when that is the target), stop and ask the user to set up the right branch first.\n- **Subproject readiness**: the target subproject exists and its dependencies are installed (e.g., `nestjs-project/node_modules` present). If not, ask the user to set it up first.\n- **Plan sanity**: the phase document has the expected structure (Step Implementations and Deliverables are required; Dependency Map is optional — if missing, the order will be derived from each SI's `Dependencies:` field). If the document looks malformed or incomplete, stop and report.\n- **Resume check**: look for a progress file (`.progress.md` sibling of the phase document). If found, read it to determine which SIs are already completed. Inform the user: \"Encontrado progress file com X/Y SIs completos. Retomando a partir de SI-NN.Z.\" If the progress file is malformed or inconsistent with the phase document, stop and report.\n\n## Execution order\n\nImplement SIs in the order defined by the **Dependency Map** in the phase document. If the Dependency Map is missing or contradicts the SIs' `Dependencies:` fields, derive the order from those fields using a topological sort — an SI can only start once all its dependencies are complete (tests passing where the SI has a Tests section).\n\nNever skip ahead. Never implement two SIs in parallel in the same run. The guarantee \"previous SI is complete (tests passing where the SI has a Tests section) before the next starts\" is the core value this skill provides; violating it defeats the purpose.\n\n## Set up the SI task list — before entering the per-SI loop\n\nBefore implementing the first SI, you **MUST** create a persistent task list that contains **one task per SI** in the phase, in the order they will be executed. Use the `TaskCreate` tool (one call per SI).\n\n- Task subject format: `SI-NN.X — <SI name>` (e.g., `SI-02.1 — HTTP Infrastructure Foundations`).\n- Task description: a one-line summary of what the SI delivers.\n- Task activeForm: what you will be doing while the SI is in progress (e.g., `Implementing HTTP infrastructure`).\n- All tasks start as `pending`.\n\nThis list is the visible plan the user can see before any code is written. It mirrors the phase document's SI sequence and serves as the execution contract for the session.\n\n**Fresh start** (no progress file found): after creating the task list, create the progress file with all SIs as `pending`.\n\n**Resume** (progress file found): after creating the task list, immediately mark already-completed SIs' tasks as `completed` (based on the progress file). The per-SI loop will skip completed SIs and start from the first `pending` one. If all SIs are already completed but the progress file's `Status` is still `in_progress`, skip the per-SI loop and proceed directly to final verification.\n\nDuring the per-SI loop:\n- Flip the current SI's task to `in_progress` when you start step 1 (Plan the SI).\n- Flip it to `completed` at the beginning of step 6, **before** emitting the per-SI completion report and the \"Seguir para SI-NN.X+1?\" question. The `TaskUpdate` and progress file update are the last tool calls allowed before the mandatory STOP in default mode (in continuous mode, the per-SI completion report is emitted, then the next SI's `TaskUpdate → in_progress` follows).\n- Never skip tasks, never batch updates — one SI's status is changed at a time.\n\nDo **not** merge multiple SIs into one task. Do **not** add ad-hoc tasks for individual technical actions — those live in the per-SI working memory (step 1), not in the persistent task list.\n\n## The per-SI loop\n\nFor each **pending** SI (completed SIs from a previous session are skipped), execute these steps in order. Do not batch them; each step's output informs the next.\n\n### 1. Plan the SI\n\nRe-read the SI section in full (Description, Technical actions, Tests, Dependencies, Acceptance criteria). Load relevant best-practices skills matching the artifacts this SI builds (e.g., `nestjs-best-practices` for modules/controllers/services, `typeorm` for entities/migrations) — load only what this SI needs, not all available skills. Keep a short internal checklist for this SI: one item per technical action; additionally, when the SI has a Tests section, one item per test file plus a \"run tests\" item. This is working memory to keep the SI on track — not a formal deliverable.\n\n### 2. Implement the technical actions\n\nWork through the technical actions in order. Stay within scope — only touch files required by **this** SI. If you notice unrelated issues (dead code, formatting, refactoring opportunities), note them for the user but do not act on them.\n\nWhen the SI introduces new dependencies, install them with the exact version ranges listed in the SI's technical actions.\n\nFollow the target subproject's conventions — read neighboring files before creating new ones so naming, structure, and style stay consistent.\n\n### 3. Write the tests\n\nIf the SI has no Tests section, skip this step and steps 4–5, and go straight to step 6 (pause). Otherwise, continue below.\n\nCreate the test files listed in the SI's Tests section. Use the testing guide skill as the reference for how to structure each layer. Each test must verify something specific the SI introduces — do not write placeholder tests.\n\nCover the SI's Acceptance Criteria. Every AC owned by this SI should be observable from at least one of this SI's tests (the AC-to-test mapping is not always 1:1, but no AC should be untestable). Note: SIs with no testable artifacts (infrastructure SIs where behavior is exercised through other SIs' tests, pure-configuration SIs, or similar) may legitimately lack a Tests section — the \"skip step 3\" branch covers all such cases.\n\n### 4. Run the tests for this SI\n\nRun **only** the test files listed in the SI's Tests section — not the full suite.\n\n### 5. Handle test failures (up to 3 fix attempts)\n\nIf tests pass on the first run, proceed to step 6 (pause).\n\nIf tests fail, enter the **fix loop**: read the failure output, diagnose the root cause, apply a focused fix, re-run the same tests. Do this at most **3 times**. Count attempts deliberately — do not lose count and loop indefinitely.\n\nFix-loop discipline:\n- **Read the error.** Do not retry blindly. If the same fix is applied twice, that's a sign the diagnosis is wrong.\n- **Fix the root cause.** Do not weaken tests to make them pass. Do not add skips, `.only`, or `xit`. Do not catch and swallow errors just to hide them.\n- **Stay in scope.** If the failure reveals a problem in a previous SI's code, stop — that's a signal to escalate, not to quietly edit a completed SI.\n- **No shortcuts.** Never disable hooks or bypass safety checks.\n\nAfter 3 unsuccessful fix attempts, **stop**. Report to the user:\n- Which SI is stuck.\n- The current test failure output (concise).\n- Your hypothesis about the root cause.\n- What you've tried.\n\nWait for the user's guidance. Do not proceed to the next SI until the user unblocks you.\n\n### 6. Pause for confirmation — STOP before the next SI\n\nThis step is a **hard stop**. After completing an SI you **MUST NOT** begin the next SI without the user's explicit approval (given per-SI in default mode, or upfront when the user requested continuous mode).\n\n- **Default mode (pause — this is the default)**: First, make a `TaskUpdate` call marking the current SI's task as `completed`, then update the progress file (mark the SI as `completed`, record test results and any out-of-scope observations noted during this SI) — these are the final tool calls permitted in this step. Then emit the per-SI completion report (SI id, name, tests passing — or `no tests` if the SI had no Tests section) and emit exactly this question as the final line of your message: **\"Seguir para SI-NN.X+1?\"** (substitute the next SI's id). Then **STOP**. Do not call any further tools. Do not start reading files for the next SI. Do not update the next SI's task to `in_progress`. Wait for the user's reply in a new turn before doing anything else.\n- **Continuous mode** (only when the user **explicitly** requested it at the start of the session with phrases like \"execute tudo\", \"autopilot\", \"don't pause between SIs\", or \"run all at once\"): Still perform the `TaskUpdate → completed` and progress file update, and emit the per-SI completion report (SI id, name, tests passing — or `no tests` if the SI had no Tests section), but **skip** the \"Seguir para SI-NN.X+1?\" question and the STOP. Then proceed directly to step 1 of the next SI. If you are unsure whether continuous mode was requested, assume default mode and pause.\n- **Last SI of the phase**: Still perform the `TaskUpdate → completed` and progress file update (same as the other modes); the per-SI completion report is folded into the phase-level Completion report (see section below), so skip the per-SI report, the question, and the STOP, and go straight to final verification.\n\nViolating this stop is the single most common failure mode of this skill. Treat \"Seguir para SI-NN.X+1?\" as a terminator, not a rhetorical question.\n\n## Final verification — after all SIs are done\n\nOnce every SI in the phase has been implemented and tested, run the phase-level checks defined in the plan's **Deliverables** checklist. These typically include:\n\n1. **Full test suite**: Run every test command listed in the plan's Deliverables (typically one for unit/integration tests and, when applicable, a separate one for E2E tests). The goal is to exercise every test in the phase together, not just the tests of a single SI.\n2. **Type-check**: Run the type-check command defined in the plan's Deliverables (e.g., `npx tsc --noEmit` for TypeScript projects).\n3. **Project build**: Run the build command defined in the project (e.g., `npm run build`) to verify the code compiles and bundles correctly.\n\nVerify any additional deliverables listed in the plan (migrations, documentation updates, seed data, configuration files). These results are presented in the **Completion report** (see section below).\n\nIf the phase spans multiple subprojects, the plan's Deliverables checklist will list these checks per subproject (e.g., `All SI tests pass in nestjs-project` and `All SI tests pass in nextjs-project`) — run each subproject's commands independently, in the order implied by the checklist.\n\nIf any final check fails, apply the same fix-loop discipline as step 5: up to 3 focused fix attempts total (shared across all failing checks, not 3 per check), re-running the affected checks after each attempt. If still failing after 3 attempts, stop and report to the user.\n\n## Completion report\n\nWhen the phase is fully done, read the progress file and generate the report:\n- Results of each deliverable check (from final verification — the only new information at this point).\n- Out-of-scope observations aggregated from the progress file (as a list of follow-ups for the user, not as things to act on).\n\nMark the progress file's `Status` as `completed`. Git operations (add, commit, push, PR) are out of scope — the user owns version control.\n\n## Rules\n\n- The phase plan is the contract. Do not add SIs, drop SIs, or change SI boundaries mid-execution. Flip each task's status exactly at the boundaries defined in step 1 (`in_progress`) and step 6 (`completed`).\n- Respect dependency order — never implement an SI whose dependencies are not yet complete (tests passing where the SI has a Tests section).\n- One SI at a time. Seu papel é de **maestro do processo**: conduzir as skills do projeto na ordem certa, revisar criticamente cada saída, refinar prompts quando o resultado vier raso, e manter os artefatos coerentes entre si.\n19\t\n20\tNa prática:\n21\t\n22\t- A investigação técnica sai da skill **`research`**.\n23\t- O plano de implementação sai da skill **`plan-phase`**.\n24\t- A implementação é conduzida pela skill **`implement-phase`**, em ciclos com teste.\n25\t- As diretrizes de teste vêm das skills **`generate-test-guide`** / **`testing-guide-nestjs-project`**.\n26\t- A verificação de integridade roda na skill **`verify-phase`**, que **você cria neste desafio**.\n27\t- Os **CLAUDE.md** são atualizados a partir do estado real do repositório.\n28\t\n29\t> As skills `research`, `plan-phase`, `implement-phase`, `generate-test-guide` e `testing-guide-nestjs-project` **já vêm no projeto e são de uso obrigatório, não as recrie**. A única skill que você cria é a `verify-phase`.\n30\t\n31\tA presença da IA precisa ser observável no repositório: skills invocadas, decisões e plano gerados, commits granulares e a sessão de Claude arquivada.\n32\t\n33\t## Objetivo\n34\t\n35\tEntregar, em um fork público do repositório base, dando continuidade ao projeto `mba-ia-greenfield-project`:\n36\t\n37\t- **Decisões técnicas** da fase, geradas pela `research` (`docs/decisions/technical-decisions-phase-06-subscriptions.md`)\n38\t- **Plano de implementação** da fase, gerado pela `plan-phase` (`docs/phases/phase-06-subscriptions.md`), no mesmo formato da `phase-02-auth.md`\n39\t- **Módulo `subscriptions/`** implementado, espelhando o módulo `auth/`, com migration, testes e suíte verde\n40\t- **Skill nova `verify-phase`** que lê o repositório e gera um relatório de integridade do processo\n41\t- **Relatório de verificação** gerado pela skill (`docs/phases/phase-06-subscriptions.verification.md`), com nota **≥ 85%**\n42\t- **CLAUDE.md** (raiz e `nestjs-project/`) atualizados com a seção de Subscriptions\n43\t- **Sessão de Claude** arquivada em `_claude-sessions/11-fase06-subscriptions.txt`\n44\t\n45\tToda informação registrada nos artefatos deve ser rastreável ao plano ou ao código. Não invente requisitos, decisões ou testes sem origem identificável.\n46\t\n47\t## Contexto\n48\t\n49\t### O que já existe no projeto\n50\t\n51\tO repositório base contém o StreamTube com as Fases 01 e 02 fechadas:\n52\t\n53\t- Backend **NestJS + TypeORM + PostgreSQL** em `nestjs-project/`, que sobe via `compose.yaml`.\n54\t- Módulo **`auth/`** completo (Module + Controller + DTOs + Service + entities + guards + e2e em `test/`). Esse é o seu **espelho arquitetural**: o módulo de subscriptions deve seguir esse mesmo formato.\n55\t- Módulos **`users/`** e **`channels/`** com Service + entidade (sem controller HTTP).\n56\t- Entidades **`User`** e **`Channel`** com relação 1:1 (cada usuário tem um canal, criado no cadastro).\n57\t- Guard JWT global (`JwtAuthGuard`) com decorators `@Public()` e `@CurrentUser()`, filtro de exceção de domínio, `ValidationPipe` global, rate limiting e migrations versionadas.\n58\t\n59\tO que **não** existe (e por isso está fora deste desafio): vídeos, upload, comentários, likes. Não há entidade, tabela ou módulo de vídeo: as Fases 03 a 05 não foram implementadas.\n60\t\n61\t### O workflow e os artefatos do curso\n62\t\n63\tO projeto adota o ciclo `research → plan → implement`, e você deve segui-lo:\n64\t\n65\t| Etapa | Skill | Artefato gerado |\n66\t|---|---|---|\n67\t| Investigar o código e decidir a abordagem | `research` | `docs/decisions/technical-decisions-phase-NN-*.md` |\n68\t| Gerar o plano executável (passos, contratos, dados) | `plan-phase` | `docs/phases/phase-NN-*.md` |\n69\t| Implementar passo a passo, rodando os testes | `implement-phase` | código + `docs/phases/phase-NN-*.progress.md` |\n70\t\n71\tConvenções do projeto que o seu trabalho precisa respeitar:\n72\t\n73\t- O plano (`phase-NN-*.md`) é organizado em **Step Implementations** com IDs no formato **`SI-NN.x`** (ex.: `SI-06.1`, `SI-06.2`), além das seções **Data Model**, **API Contracts**, **Authorization Matrix**, **Error Catalog**, **Dependency Map** e **Deliverables**. Use a `phase-02-auth.md` como referência de formato.\n74\t- Os **commits são granulares por SI**, no formato real do projeto: `Implementando SI-06.x: <descrição>`.\n75\t- O **`phase-NN-*.progress.md`** é o log de progresso por SI (status, testes que passaram, observações), mantido durante a implementação.\n76\t- As skills ficam em **`.claude/skills/<nome>/SKILL.md`** (maiúsculo), com frontmatter `name`, `description` e `disable-model-invocation: true`.\n77\t\n78\t> **Atenção a um detalhe que reprova:** o `progress.md` já tem um significado no projeto (log de SIs). O relatório da sua skill de verificação é um arquivo **diferente** (`.verification.md`): não sobrescreva nem reaproveite o `progress.md`.\n79\t\n80\t## Escopo da feature: Inscrição em Canais\n81\t\n82\tVocê vai implementar o seguinte, e nada além disso:\n83\t\n84\t**Comportamento**\n85\t\n86\t- Um usuário autenticado pode **se inscrever** em um canal e **cancelar a inscrição**.\n87\t- Um usuário pode **listar os canais que segue**.\n88\t- Um canal expõe a sua **contagem de inscritos**.\n89\t\n90\t**Endpoints** (todos autenticados, reusando o `JwtAuthGuard` global)\n91\t\n92\t- `POST   /channels/:channelId/subscription`: inscrever-se\n93\t- `DELETE /channels/:channelId/subscription`: cancelar inscrição\n94\t- `GET    /me/subscriptions`: listar canais que o usuário segue\n95\t- contagem de inscritos exposta na resposta do canal (defina a forma exata no plano)\n96\t\n97\t**Regras de negócio e edge cases** (refine e numere no plano via `plan-phase`)\n98\t\n99\t- Inscrição é única por par **(usuário, canal)**, garantida por *unique constraint* no banco.\n100\t- Um usuário **não pode se inscrever no próprio canal**.\n101\t- **Inscrição duplicada** e **cancelamento de inscrição inexistente**: defina o comportamento (idempotente vs. conflito/erro) na `research` e justifique.\n102\t- **Canal inexistente** → 404.\n103\t- Comportamento para **usuário não confirmado** (`is_confirmed = false`): decida e documente.\n104\t- A listagem de inscrições **não pode ter problema de N+1** (carregue o canal junto), alinhado à rule `db-avoid-n-plus-one`.\n105\t\n106\t**Persistência**\n107\t\n108\t- Nova entidade **`Subscription`** → tabela **`subscriptions`**: `id` (uuid), `user_id` (uuid, FK → users), `channel_id` (uuid, FK → channels), `created_at`. *Unique* em `(user_id, channel_id)`; índices em `user_id` e `channel_id`.\n109\t- **Migration TypeORM** criando a tabela, no padrão das migrations existentes.\n110\t\n111\t> Esse recorte mapeia direto em três entregáveis da Fase 06 do plano original: *\"inscrição em canais (seguir/deixar de seguir)\"*, *\"área de canais seguidos\"* e *\"contagem de inscritos na página do canal\"*.\n112\t\n113\t## Requisitos\n114\t\n115\t### 1. Decisões técnicas (via `research`)\n116\t\n117\tRode a skill **`research`** sobre o código existente para mapear os pontos de integração (entidades `User`/`Channel`, guard JWT, padrão de service/repository, filtro de exceções) e decidir a abordagem da feature. Salve o resultado em `docs/decisions/technical-decisions-phase-06-subscriptions.md`.\n118\t\n119\tAs decisões em aberto do escopo (inscrição duplicada, cancelamento inexistente, usuário não confirmado, forma de expor a contagem) devem ser **decididas e justificadas aqui**: é esse documento que alimenta o plano.\n120\t\n121\t### 2. Plano de implementação (via `plan-phase`)\n122\t\n123\tInvoque a skill **`plan-phase`** a partir das decisões. Salve em `docs/phases/phase-06-subscriptions.md`, **espelhando o formato da `phase-02-auth.md`**:\n124\t\n125\t- Objetivo\n126\t- **Step Implementations** (`SI-06.1`, `SI-06.2`, …) com ações e arquivos a criar/tocar\n127\t- **Data Model** (tabela `subscriptions`, constraints, índices)\n128\t- **API Contracts** (cada endpoint com payload de exemplo e status codes)\n129\t- **Authorization Matrix**\n130\t- **Error Catalog**\n131\t- **Dependency Map** e **Deliverables**\n132\t\n133\t> Revise criticamente a saída crua da skill. Normalmente são necessárias 1 a 2 iterações: contratos vagos, SIs grandes demais ou dependências fora de ordem envenenam a implementação.\n134\t\n135\t### 3. Implementação (via `implement-phase` + testes)\n136\t\n137\tImplemente o módulo em `nestjs-project/src/subscriptions/`, **espelhando o módulo `auth/`** e conduzido pela skill **`implement-phase`** (que executa SI a SI e só avança com os testes do SI passando).\n138\t\n139\tA organização concreta de arquivos é **decisão do seu plano** (saída da `plan-phase`), não algo que este enunciado entrega pronto: definir a estrutura faz parte do que o desafio avalia. A regra é **consistência arquitetural com o `auth/`**: a mesma divisão em camadas (Module, Controller, Service, DTOs, entidade) e os mesmos tipos de teste que o `auth/` tem: unit (`.spec`), integração (`.integration-spec`) e e2e em `test/`. Investigue o `auth/` na etapa de research e deixe o plano definir os arquivos exatos. Siga também as convenções do projeto para onde vivem a migration (`src/database/migrations/`) e o teste e2e (`test/`).\n140\t\n141\tIndependentemente da estrutura que o plano definir, estes artefatos são **inegociáveis** (e cobrados nos Critérios de Aceite): o módulo registrado, um controller com os endpoints, um service com testes unit e de integração, a entidade `Subscription`, o teste e2e da feature e a migration criando a tabela `subscriptions` com *unique* em `(user_id, channel_id)`.\n142\t\n143\tDisciplina de implementação (a mesma do projeto do professor):\n144\t\n145\t- **Commits granulares por SI**, no formato `Implementando SI-06.x: <descrição>`. Um commit único gigante (`feat: subscriptions`) reprova.\n146\t- Cada SI com comportamento testável tem **testes** (unit no `.spec`, integração no `.integration-spec`), registrados no `progress.md`.\n147\t- **Testes de integração e e2e usam o PostgreSQL real** do `compose.yaml`: **não mocke o TypeORM** em teste de integração.\n148\t- Mantenha o **`docs/phases/phase-06-subscriptions.progress.md`** atualizado (status + testes por SI), como na Fase 02.\n149\t\n150\t### 4. Skill nova: `verify-phase`\n151\t\n152\t**Por que você cria essa skill.** Num workflow tocado por IA, o agente produz muito e rápido, e é fácil um passo escapar sem ninguém perceber: um SI planejado que nunca foi implementado, código que subiu sem teste, um commit citando um passo que não existe, ou o `progress.md` dizendo uma coisa e o código outra. Conferir isso na mão, no fim de cada fase, é lento e sujeito a erro. A `verify-phase` é um **portão de QA reutilizável**: cruza as fontes de verdade do processo (plano, commits, progress e código/testes) e responde, de forma objetiva, se o que você entregou bate com o que você planejou, e onde estão os furos. Com isso, ela fecha o pilar de **Skills** do curso: você usou skills que *produzem* o trabalho (research, plan, implement) e agora cria uma que *governa a qualidade* dele. Repare que ela não duplica a `implement-phase`: aquela executa pra frente, garantindo teste verde enquanto avança; a `verify-phase` audita o estado final pra trás, plano contra entregue.\n153\t\n154\tCrie a skill em **`.claude/skills/verify-phase/SKILL.md`** (na raiz do projeto, não dentro de `nestjs-project/`). Ela **não duplica** nenhuma skill existente: enquanto as outras *produzem* a fase, esta **mede a integridade do processo** que você executou.\n155\t\n156\tInvocação:\n157\t\n158\t```bash\n159\tclaude \"/verify-phase phase-06-subscriptions\"\n160\t```\n161\t\n162\tA skill **lê o repositório (somente leitura)** e cruza as fontes da fase:\n163\t\n164\t1. O **plano** (`docs/phases/<fase>.md`): extrai os `SI-NN.x`, os arquivos esperados e os critérios de aceite.\n165\t2. O **git log** da fase: extrai os `SI-NN.x` referenciados nos commits.\n166\t3. O **progress.md** (`docs/phases/<fase>.progress.md`): status e testes por SI.\n167\t4. O **código e os testes** em disco: confere se os arquivos previstos pelo plano existem.\n168\t5. O **estado da suíte**: se os SIs com testes estão verdes (lê o `progress.md`; opcionalmente executa a suíte).\n169\t\n170\tE gera **`docs/phases/<fase>.verification.md`** neste formato:\n171\t\n172\t```markdown\n173\t# Fase 06: Relatório de Integridade do Processo\n174\t\n175\t## Nota de Integridade\n176\t88%  STATUS: APROVADO  (corte: ≥ 85%)\n177\t\n178\t## Matriz de Cobertura\n179\t| Dimensão                       | Cobertura | Detalhe                      |\n180\t|--------------------------------|-----------|------------------------------|\n181\t| Plano → Commits (SI)           | 7/7       | ✓                            |\n182\t| SI → Progress                  | 7/7       | ✓                            |\n183\t| Arquivos previstos             | 11/12     | ⚠ falta o e2e do unsubscribe |\n184\t| Suíte de testes                | verde     | ✓                            |\n185\t| Refs órfãos (SI fora do plano) | 0         | ✓                            |\n186\t\n187\t## Gaps detectados\n188\t- [MED] SI-06.5 sem teste e2e correspondente\n189\t\n190\t## Recomendações\n191\t1. Adicione o e2e do cancelamento de inscrição\n192\t```\n193\t\n194\t**Cálculo da nota** (defina os pesos em um arquivo de referência da skill; sugestão):\n195\t\n196\t```\n197\tNota = (\n198\t    Plano_Commits   * 0.25 +\n199\t    SI_Progress     * 0.20 +\n200\t    Arquivos        * 0.25 +\n201\t    Suite_verde     * 0.20 +\n202\t    (1 - Refs_orfaos_ratio) * 0.10\n203\t) * 100\n204\t```\n205\t\n206\tRequisitos da skill:\n207\t\n208\t- **Frontmatter** com `name`, `description` e `disable-model-invocation: true` (padrão das skills do projeto).\n209\t- **Agnóstica de fase**: recebe o nome da fase como argumento e funciona para `phase-02-auth`, `phase-06-subscriptions` etc.\n210\t- **Somente leitura** sobre o repositório: só escreve o `.verification.md`.\n211\t- Detecta IDs com regex robusto: `\\bSI-\\d{2}\\.\\d+\\b`.\n212\t- O `SKILL.md` **é um prompt, não um programa**: descreva o procedimento e a ordem, e use arquivos de referência (template do relatório, regex, pesos) para ancorar o comportamento.\n213\t\n214\t> **Teste a skill com o repo \"vazio\" também.** Ela tem que rodar mesmo antes da implementação: a nota é que vai ser baixa. Se ela quebra sem implementação, o bug é na skill, não no repo.\n215\t\n216\t### 5. Verificação e correção de gaps\n217\t\n218\tDepois de implementar, rode `claude \"/verify-phase phase-06-subscriptions\"`. **Se a nota ficar abaixo de 85%, corrija os gaps no repositório e rode de novo**: é esperado iterar 2 a 3 vezes. A versão final do `.verification.md` commitada é o relatório avaliado.\n219\t\n220\t> A nota sobe **corrigindo o repositório**, não editando o relatório à mão. O avaliador pode re-rodar a sua skill; se o relatório no repo divergir do que a skill produz, reprova.\n221\t\n222\t### 6. Atualização dos CLAUDE.md\n223\t\n224\tAtualize `CLAUDE.md` (raiz) e `nestjs-project/CLAUDE.md` com a seção de Subscriptions, refletindo o estado real do código:\n225\t\n226\t```markdown\n227\t## Subscriptions (Fase 06, recorte)\n228\t- Endpoints: POST/DELETE /channels/:id/subscription, GET /me/subscriptions\n229\t- Regra: 1 inscrição por (usuário, canal); sem auto-inscrição\n230\t- Plano: docs/phases/phase-06-subscriptions.md\n231\t- Verificação: docs/phases/phase-06-subscriptions.verification.md\n232\t- Testes: src/subscriptions/**/*.spec.ts + test/subscriptions.e2e-spec.ts\n233\t```\n234\t\n235\t`CLAUDE.md` que cite arquivos ou comportamentos inexistentes reprova.\n236\t\n237\t### 7. Sessão arquivada\n238\t\n239\tExporte a sessão principal de Claude Code para `_claude-sessions/11-fase06-subscriptions.txt` (bruto serve). É evidência secundária, usada pelo avaliador em caso de divergência entre o repositório e o relatório.\n240\t\n241\t## Critérios de Aceite\n242\t\n243\tTodos obrigatórios. Esta é a lista única de avaliação: os requisitos não se repetem em outra seção.\n244\t\n245\t**Decisões e plano**\n246\t\n247\t- [ ] `technical-decisions-phase-06-subscriptions.md` gerado pela `research`, com as decisões em aberto resolvidas e justificadas\n248\t- [ ] `phase-06-subscriptions.md` gerado pela `plan-phase`, no formato da `phase-02-auth.md` (SIs `SI-06.x`, Data Model, API Contracts, Authorization Matrix, Error Catalog, Deliverables)\n249\t\n250\t**Implementação**\n251\t\n252\t- [ ] Módulo `subscriptions/` no padrão de `auth/` (Module + Controller + DTO + Service + APROVADO\n274\t- [ ] `CLAUDE.md` raiz e `nestjs-project/` com a seção Subscriptions, coerentes com o código\n275\t- [ ] `_claude-sessions/11-fase06-subscriptions.txt` presente\n276\t\n277\t## Reprova automática\n278\t\n279\t- ❌ Implementar sem usar as skills `research`, `plan-phase` e `implement-phase`\n280\t- ❌ Commit único gigante ou sem referência ao SI\n281\t- ❌ Plano que não segue o formato da `phase-02-auth.md` (sem SIs, sem contratos)\n282\t- ❌ Mockar o TypeORM em teste de integração\n283\t- ❌ Skill `verify-phase` sem frontmatter, que não roda, ou que escreve fora do `.verification.md`\n284\t- ❌ Reaproveitar/sobrescrever o `progress.md` como relatório de verificação\n285\t- ❌ Nota de integridade < 85%, ou `.verification.md` escrito à mão\n286\t- ❌ `CLAUDE.md` inconsistente com o código\n287\t- ❌ Inventar vídeos, likes ou comentários: fora do escopo (não existem no projeto)\n288\t\n289\t## Estrutura do entregável\n290\t\n291\tTudo dentro do fork do `mba-ia-greenfield-project`. índices em `user_id` e `channel_id`.\n- **Migration TypeORM** criando a tabela, no padrão das migrations existentes.\n\n> Esse recorte mapeia direto em três entregáveis da Fase 06 do plano original: *\"inscrição em canais (seguir/deixar de seguir)\"*, *\"área de canais seguidos\"* e *\"contagem de inscritos na página do canal\"*.\n\n## Requisitos\n\n### 1. Skill nova: `verify-phase`\n\n**Por que você cria essa skill.** Num workflow tocado por IA, o agente produz muito e rápido, e é fácil um passo escapar sem ninguém perceber: um SI planejado que nunca foi implementado, código que subiu sem teste, um commit citando um passo que não existe, ou o `progress.md` dizendo uma coisa e o código outra. Conferir isso na mão, no fim de cada fase, é lento e sujeito a erro. A `verify-phase` é um **portão de QA reutilizável**: cruza as fontes de verdade do processo (plano, commits, progress e código/testes) e responde, de forma objetiva, se o que você entregou bate com o que você planejou, e onde estão os furos. Com isso, ela fecha o pilar de **Skills** do curso: você usou skills que *produzem* o trabalho (research, plan, implement) e agora cria uma que *governa a qualidade* dele. Repare que ela não duplica a `implement-phase`: aquela executa pra frente, garantindo teste verde enquanto avança; a `verify-phase` audita o estado final pra trás, plano contra entregue.\n\nCrie a skill em **`.claude/skills/verify-phase/SKILL.md`** (na raiz do projeto, não dentro de `nestjs-project/`). If not found, throw `InvalidTokenException`. If expired (`expires_at < now`), throw `TokenExpiredException`. If revoked (`revoked_at IS NOT NULL`): check grace period — if `(now - revoked_at) <= 10 seconds`, find the latest non-revoked token in the same family and return a new access token paired with that token (do not create yet another token); if `(now - revoked_at) > 10 seconds`, this is reuse — revoke ALL tokens in the family (`UPDATE refresh_tokens SET revoked_at = now WHERE family = :family AND revoked_at IS NULL`), throw `TokenReuseDetectedException`. If valid: revoke current token (`revoked_at = now`), generate new JWT refresh token in the same family (same `family` UUID, new `jti`), store its SHA-256 hash in `refresh_tokens`, generate new access token, return both\n286\t- Create `src/auth/dto/refresh-token.dto.ts` — `RefreshTokenDto` with `@IsString() @IsNotEmpty()` refresh_token\n287\t- Add `@Public() @Post('refresh')` to `AuthController` — accepts `{ refresh_token }`, returns 200 with `{ access_token, refresh_token }`\n288\t\n289\t**Tests:**\n290\t\n291\t| File | Layer | Verifies |\n292\t|------|-------|----------|\n293\t| `src/auth/auth.service.spec.ts` | Unit | Refresh: valid token rotates, expired rejects, reuse within grace period returns latest token, reuse beyond grace period revokes family |\n294\t| `src/auth/auth.service.integration-spec.ts` | Integration | Rotation persists new token and revokes old; family revocation updates all tokens in family |\n295\t| `test/auth.e2e-spec.ts` | E2E | `POST /auth/refresh` 200 with rotated tokens, 401 on invalid/expired, 401 with `TOKEN_REUSE_DETECTED` on reused token |\n296\t\n297\t**Dependencies:** SI-02.8\n298\t\n299\t**Acceptance criteria:**\n300\t\n301\t- `POST /auth/refresh` with a valid refresh token returns 200 with new `{ access_token, refresh_token }`; (SI-02.6)\n598\t\n599\t**Request headers:**\n600\t- Content-Type: application/json\n601\t\n602\t**Request body:**\n603\t- email: string, required — valid email format\n604\t- password: string, required — min 8, max 128 characters\n605\t\n606\t**Response 201:**\n607\t- id: string (uuid)\n608\t- email: string\n609\t\n610\t**Error responses:**\n611\t- 409 EMAIL_ALREADY_EXISTS: when the email SI-02.17)\n617\t\n618\t**Request query parameters:**\n619\t- token: string, required — the raw hex token from the confirmation email\n620\t\n621\t**Response 204:** No content.\n622\t\n623\t**Error responses:**\n624\t- 401 INVALID_TOKEN: when the token is not found or already used\n625\t- 401 TOKEN_EXPIRED: when the token has expired\n626\t- 400 validation error: when `token` query parameter is missing or empty\n627\t\n628\t---\n629\t\n630\t#### POST /auth/resend-confirmation (SI-02.7)\n631\t\n632\t**Request headers:**\n633\t- Content-Type: application/json\n634\t\n635\t**Request body:**\n636\t- email: string, required — valid email format\n637\t\n638\t**Response 204:** No content.\n639\t\n640\t**Error responses:**\n641\t- 400 validation error: when the request body fails schema validation\n642\t\n643\t---\n644\t\n645\t#### POST /auth/login (SI-02.8)\n646\t\n647\t**Request headers:**\n648\t- Content-Type: application/json\n649\t\n650\t**Request body:**\n651\t- email: string, required — valid email format\n652\t- password: string, required — non-empty\n653\t\n654\t**Response 200:**\n655\t- access_token: string (JWT)\n656\t- refresh_token: string (JWT)\n657\t\n658\t**Error responses:**\n659\t- 401 INVALID_CREDENTIALS: when email does not exist OR password is wrong (same error for both)\n660\t- 403 EMAIL_NOT_CONFIRMED: when the user's email has string (JWT)\n675\t- refresh_token: string (new JWT refresh token)\n676\t\n677\t**Error responses:**\n678\t- 401 INVALID_TOKEN: when the token is not found\n679\t- 401 TOKEN_EXPIRED: when the token
